MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday I asked the Minister of Agriculture the following question, as reported at page 1609 of Hansard of that date:
In view of the extremely low market price of 6 cents per pound paid to British Columbia raspberry producers, will the minister consider bringing raspberries under the price stabilization act to enable these producers to take off their present crop?
In his reply the minister commented that I had been back in the northern fastness too long because this matter, he claimed, had been dealt with previously.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: He was wrong; you have been here too long.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I am going to be here a lot longer, too.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: That's what you think.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I suggest that the minister himself has been wandering around some place other than his office, because-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: Order. Would the hon. member state his question of privilege?

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, before I asked the question yesterday I checked with the officials concerned and found that no decision had been taken on the question of placing a price support under raspberries. The minister's answer, then, in my opinion was both arrogant and completely false.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: Order. I am sure the hon. member would not like to leave that statement standing on the record.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I think after I get through you will see why I leave it on the record.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I am asking the hon. member to withdraw it.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: If I have to withdraw it, I will have to withdraw it.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: That is no way to do it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext:
May I say that while the hon. member may not agree with what the minister said, and even if one assumes that
the minister was mistaken, that does not to my mind raise a question of privilege.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: Surely it is a question of privilege if he misled the house.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: My question of privilege is this, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture deliberately misled the house in reply to my question.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: Withdraw that.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all I think the hon. member should withdraw his statement that I deliberately misled the house, because I state unequivocally that his comment is completely incorrect. I did not mislead the house yesterday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: The hon. member has heard what the minister has said, and he knows the practice of the house-that it is quite outside of our accepted standards of conduct here to impute to another hon. member the deliberate statement of falsehood or untruth. The words which the hon. member has used do just that, and I must ask him if he will withdraw them.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I will withdraw that statement, Mr. Speaker, but I will not withdraw the implication I made that the minister was not informed as to what took place in his own department.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I think the hon. member has sufficiently made his point that he disagrees with what the minister said yesterday; and as he has withdrawn the statement, unless there is a question of privilege I do not think he should proceed further.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: The minister claimed yesterday in reply to my question that the matter had been dealt with the week before. I find this morning that a recommendation had been signed by him this morning and up until noon today a quorum of four of the cabinet ministers had not approved this recommendation and the order in council had not been passed, at least up until noon today.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member would raise the matter as a question at the appropriate time. As I have said before, it does not seem to me to be a question of privilege.
1640	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been raised as a question of privilege, and I would like to reply to it on a question of privilege. The statement I made yesterday was absolutely correct. The stabilization board sent a wire under my instructions, and after having received the approval of cabinet, to the processors of raspberries in British Columbia. The wire was sent on Thursday night last, making a proposition or an offer to them. As far as the support of raspberries was concerned, it provided that they had to pay a minimum of 9 cents a pound to the growers. They had a meeting on Friday morning and wired back accepting this offer, and I immediately gave instructions to wire back to them to put this 9-cent price into effect immediately. That is the exact situation.

On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if he would table the telegrams referred to by him in his reply earlier today to the hon. member for Mackenzie River, and if he would also at the same time table the order in council referred to?

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: I would be quite happy to table the telegrams and also the order in council, but of course the order in council appears in the normal form of the Canada Gazette.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to avoid any further misunderstanding or mistakes on the part of the official opposition in connection with the question of raspberries in British Columbia perhaps I should say an additional word or two on the subject.
The matter first came up something like ten days to two weeks ago. A considerable number of telegrams were received here from raspberry growers stating that they were threatened with a very low price and asking for some form of support. The matter was particularly brought to my attention by the hon. members for Fraser Valley and New Westminster. We canvassed the situation and had a senior official of the department in British Columbia investigate the matter. At about the time the investigation concluded as to what the probable situation would be, the first of the raspberries began to come on the market and the processors of these raspberries who put them into S02 or freeze them were offering 6 cents a pound for this fruit.
As a result I took up the matter and obtained cabinet approval, as 1 indicated before,


to make an offer to the processors which would ensure that the growers received a minimum of 9 cents a pound. I then dispatched the telegram I mentioned a short time ago.
That is the whole situation. The order in council which provides the specific terms under which the processors will be paid in the event they cannot dispose of the raspberries put into S02 and held in frozen form was signed today. It went through today but the actual action, as I indicated, was taken last Thursday and Friday, and the growers were thus put in a position to sell their raspberries at a minimum of 9 cents last week, as I stated in the house yesterday.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture raises quite an important question of privilege. I believe the house will be very glad of the statement he just made clarifying this matter, but I feel I must fulfil my obligation of pointing out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the minister in answer to the question yesterday, as recorded at page 1609 of Hansard, said:
I think perhaps he-
That is the hon. member for Mackenzie River.
-has been back in the northern fastness too long, because this matter was dealt with last week.
Note these remarks, Mr. Speaker:
Assistance was provided under the stabilization act for the raspberry growers in British Columbia which will ensure that they will be paid a minimum of 9 cents per pound for the poorest type of raspberry which is produced there.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, the statement that assistance was provided.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: It was.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: They pay no attention to such things as orders in council.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: The act provides that these things are done by order in council, and hon. members are entitled to know that the law of this country is being observed. At this stage of the proceedings today the minister has told us that the order in council was passed this day, but yesterday he said that the assistance was provided under the act last week.

subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext: And the minister used to talk about C. D. Howe.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HARDIE    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE OF JUNE 25
speechtext:
I did not know so much heat could be generated over a raspberry. I think the hon. member for Ottawa West is within his rights, of course, in raising a question of privilege if he feels that the information given to the house by the hon. minister was incorrect, but I must say that having heard everything that was said today the problem seems to be one of interpretation of what the minister said yesterday and of what it meant. Everyone is entitled to put his own construction on it. I think the matter has been sufficiently aired.
I see that the hon. member for Kootenay West is on his feet. Is this on the point of privilege?

Mr. Speaker. In order to avoid any further misunderstanding in connection with the application of this most important legislation, would the minister make an announcement to the house when the application of the British Columbia tree fruit growers for support prices for the 1957 crop is granted?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Justice, with some restrained indignation. In view of the very disturbing tale in the Printed Word, a periodical published by the public relations firm of Johnston, Everson and Charlesworth Limited, to this effect:
When President Truman visited Ottawa at the end of the war, his guards searched, without warrant, every house along the line of march, including clothes closets, attics and cellars-
-would the Minister of Justice (1) make inquiries as to the veracity of this report and later inform the house as to the result; (2) assure the house that such procedure will not be countenanced in Canada, at any time, for any purpose, and that the basic rights and freedoms of Canadians will be recognized and respected on all such occasions?
1642	HOUSE OF

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SECURITY MEASURES DURING VISITS OF HEADS OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rather doubt whether an allegation about a matter that took place some 10 or 11 years ago, as the visit of President Truman did, is one of sufficient or immediate urgency to justify an inquiry on the orders of the day. However, I have had some inquiry made-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SECURITY MEASURES DURING VISITS OF HEADS OF STATE
speechtext:
Order. If the minister is
raising that as a point of order I would agree with him that the first part of the question might be dealt with differently, but the second part of the question remains.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SECURITY MEASURES DURING VISITS OF HEADS OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. I can assure the hon. gentleman, as a result of inquiries I have made and discussions I have had with those connected with such matters that there is no likelihood of any such event taking place in connection with any future visit by any head of state who visits Canada. I am also able to say, since the matter has been raised, that the inquiries I have made indicate, so far as my present information goes, that the report of the incidents in connection with the previous visit to which the hon. gentleman has referred is greatly exaggerated, certainly in so far as any allegation of the searching of every private house along the route is concerned.

subtopic: SECURITY MEASURES DURING VISITS OF HEADS OF STATE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: KETTLE VALLEY, B.C.-STATEMENT ON TRANSPORTATION OF PERSONS HAVING COMMUNICABLE DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday the hon.
57071-3-104J
Inquiries of the Ministry member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) inquired as to the transporting of patients suffering from communicable diseases by railway in the Kettle valley area. In putting his question the hon. member stated that a certain hospital in Kootenay West had been informed by the legal officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway that persons suffering from communicable diseases may ride in the baggage section of the present Budd cars on the Kettle valley line.
If the hospital referred to by my hon. friend is the same hospital which made representations direct to the board of transport commissioners on this point, I think there must be some misunderstanding of the reply made to those representations by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
I am advised that Mr. E. M. Stiles, chairman of the board of the Kootenay Lake general hospital society, Nelson, wrote to the board of transport commissioners under date of April 28. The railway company was asked for its submissions, and the legal department of the railway pointed out in reply that rail diesel cars do not provide separate or private accommodation of any kind but that it is permissible to carry stretchers with sick persons in the baggage portion of the rail diesel car provided they are accompanied by another person.
The letter went on to state, however, that this permission has been restricted to persons who are suffering from non-communicable diseases. The letter added that general order No. 804 of the board of transport commissioners requires that if there is no other enclosed accommodation on a train, a person suffering from a communicable disease can be handled in the baggage car; but as the baggage section is part of the rail diesel car and is occupied by the train baggageman and the news agent, it is not considered that such cases should be handled.
I am advised that a copy of the reply from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was sent to Mr. Stiles.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday as reported at page 1609 of Hansard the hon. member for Levis referred to a story carried in the Toronto Star of June 24 with regard to the Canadian pavilion at the world's trade fair at Brussels. His question was as follows:
-has the minister, as alleged in the newspaper story, curtly accepted the resignation of Madame Valmore Bienvenue, chaperone of the university students who are acting as guides at the Canadian pavilion, and would the minister comment on the whole situation?
I have seen the story in the Toronto Star. I did not curtly but, rather, courteously accepted the resignation of Madame Bienvenue, which I judged was put before me in good faith, and I apprized her of our appreciation of her services. I had no knowledge that there was anything more to it than that.
The story in the Star talks about low morale. My information is that the morale among the students over there is very high. Visitors who have been attending the exhibition have reported largely that the Canadian pavilion is a credit to Canada. Some have said otherwise, but most of the reports I have received recently say that it is a credit to Canada; that the European visitors are impressed with the exhibit, and that the student guides are good representatives of our country. They are enjoying a remarkably fine experience in being chosen to spend about six months in Europe, the type of experience that almost any university student would like to have, and I think they are a credit to Canada. I know of no low morale on the part of any members of the staff whatsoever. Some difficulties may arise from time to time which I think are insignificant.
May I say this with regard to the exhibit over there. The Toronto Star story says something about lack of funds. That exhibit has cost about $3 million. Other countries exhibiting at the world's fair are spending $18 million or over $20 million on their exhibits and, of course, we do not expect to compete in a circle of that size. But if you compare the Canadian exhibit with that

of countries of similar size and wealth I think you will find that it is quite satisfactory to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the end of yesterday's sitting I was saying that my constituency is extremely rich in mineral resources, and I am now happy to announce to the house that uranium deposits have been discovered quite recently in northern Timiskaming in the Kippewa and Hunter's Point area, and that these deposits, according to experts, bid fair to be among the richest in the land.
I was particularly happy to learn, while listening to the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), that the government intends to take steps to continue and increase the assistance to gold 57071-3-105
The Budget-Mr. Martineau mines. I was all the happier to learn this because in my constituency there is one extremely rich gold mine, the Belleterre mine, which has been in production for close to 20 years. I submit that the government should look after the problems which beset gold producers, not only by continuing to grant subsidies, but by increasing them. That is, of course no permanent solution but to my mind, every time the occasion offers, representations should be made to the American government for an increase in the price of gold. In this connection, I fully agree with my colleague the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Martel) who requested the Canadian government to take such steps as are necessary so that the price of that product may be increased. I do not believe it is an exaggeration to state that, at this time, the price of gold should be set at $75 an ounce.
Mr. Speaker, among the budget resolutions, that which refers to public works is particularly noteworthy. To my mind we should not be content with a single huge operation in a single, possibly unexplored, area, but money should be voted towards public works in the populated areas of this country, where there could be unemployment. Such works would be of benefit to localities which need the suggested improvements and would also help to relieve local unemployment. (Text):
I have reviewed some of the problems pertaining to the northern section of my riding, the county of Timiskaming, and I should like to speak briefly now about some of the problems that beset the southern section of the riding, the county of Pontiac. The population of the county of Pontiac is made up principally of farmers, workers in the forest and lumbering industries, and miners. I have dealt with farmers throughout Pontiac county for quite a number of years, and I remember how in the last years of the Liberal regime farmers would come up to me and say, "Well, we are just hanging on. We do not know how long we can still hang on, because the situation is bad and is getting worse."
The present government has been in power for approximately one year but the farmers I see today, who are engaged in dairy farming and mixed farming, tell me they are well satisfied with the measures adopted so far by the government. They say these measures have contributed in a real sense to the betterment of their condition, and they tell me that all we have to do is to continue

The Budget-Mr. Martineau in that vein and the farming section of our population will certainly always be grateful to the government.
Speaking about improvement in the lot of the farmers, I think of the many "gloom doomers" on the other side of the house-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-who have been talking about a slump, about a recession, and about the so-called horrible calamities that have beset the country since, due to unfortunate circumstances, they are no longer the leaders of the country. I really think their zeal is most touching but it is certainly not convincing, especially if one analyses their statements in the light of the plight of the farmers, particularly small farmers such as we have in my riding, who as a class were really completely neglected under the former administration.
In the county of Pontiac we have some very good fairs which are organized each year by the farmers. I believe the outstanding one among them is the Shawville fair, an event which has taken place every year for over 100 years. The farmers of the Shawville area and Pontiac county generally are indeed very pleased to know that the Minister of Agriculture will be able to open the fair in September. Tomorrow another agricultural fair is opening at Quyon, and it will last a couple of days. I take this occasion to invite any of my colleagues who have a bit of time on their hands or who would like a restful change to drive the 30-odd scenic miles up to Pontiac county and visit that fair. I am quite sure they will find it most enjoyable. A little later the Chapeau fair will be held, also one of the outstanding agricultural events of our county.
I am pleased to say that some of the exhibits at these fairs have won wide acclaim and first prizes at some of our national fairs, such as the Royal winter fair. The government has given generous grants to some of these fairs, but I suggest that wherever possible the grants should be increased. It is money that is certainly well spent, and it goes far to promote interest in agricultural events.
As in the county of Timiskaming so in the county of Pontiac there is a crying need for a public investment program. This need is all the more crying in that the county was neglected for a great number of years. There are urgent public works projects that should be initiated and soon. Some of them, such as the construction of the new Bryson bridge, are long overdue. There is a very dangerous situation for the users of that bridge, and I suggest that all measures that may be taken


should now be taken without delay to see that this much needed bridge is constructed, as the present structure has proved completely inadequate to carry the traffic which has to go over it.
Other bridges are also needed in the county. I shall mention only two. A bridge is needed from Quyon to Fitzroy Harbour and a new bridge is needed at Chapeau, Quebec. So far as the Quyon bridge is concerned, I believe that such a project could be incorporated into the national capital plan. It was with great gratification that I learned that the government had decided to acquire the green belt on the outskirts of Ottawa. While on that subject, I think Gatineau park, some of which lies within my constituency, should be enlarged. The Quyon bridge could probably then be incorporated in the larger national capital area.
The development of the national capital is perhaps not something for the immediate future, but I believe that in the course of the next decade the city of Ottawa is slated to become one of the great capitals of the world.
I remember coming to Ottawa as a student in the pre-war years, perhaps 20 years ago, and at that time Ottawa was still a kind of village. It may have been a big village but it was still a village, and I am just amazed at the progress which has taken place here during the last 10 years. Ottawa is truly becoming one of the great cities of this country and if we consider the development which has taken place in just one decade-having in mind that 10 years is a very small period of time in the life of a city and still less in the life of a country-we can surely envisage in the not too distant future a city of surpassing beauty on the banks of the Ottawa river.
It therefore behooves the government to look toward those days. I know steps have been taken, but I think the field of activity and progress should be widened so that Ottawa will acquire a green belt and there will be set aside large areas as national park lands in order to complete the national capital program.
It is in this larger area which I have in mind that I believe my own constituency of Pontiac-Timiskaming can play its part because, judging from the opinions of the many tourists who visit us each year, my constituency is one of the beauty spots of Canada. Yet at the present time it lacks tourist accommodation, and I think some consideration should be given by the government with respect to aid to the operators of tourist resorts. The government has already announced that it will bring forward legislation to help small businessmen. I believe

the tourist resort operators should be included in that group, and that their needs should be considered since they do bring considerable sums of money into Canada. In this way my county will have an opportunity to become outstanding, because from the point of view of natural beauty it has all that it takes to become a great tourist attraction.
I have examined the criticisms of the budget in the speeches of hon. members, most of which I actually heard delivered in the house. All I can see in these criticisms is a lot of contradictions, whining and groaning. The critics have singled out the huge deficit, as they call it, and have also talked about unemployment. I do not see why hon. members of the opposition should be particularly alarmed about deficit financing; as a matter of fact practically every minister of finance during the long Liberal regime spoke about cyclical budgetting. They stated that in times of prosperity one had to accumulate a surplus, and that when there was a pause one should not hesitate to have a deficit as a sort of pump primer to the economic wheel. Why should they now deny what they previously accepted as a sacred economic principle? They say there is now a pause, they say there is a recession, and they apply all their energies to exaggerating that condition.
There is, as the Minister of Finance has said, a slackening in the expansion of our economic activity, but there is no desperate crisis such as the members of the opposition would have us believe. In that connection I can truthfully say that in the county of Pontiac there is this year more employment than for a long time, and from reports in the newspapers during the last few days it would seem to me that the members of the opposition have lost 150,000 reasons for their whining and groaning.
I say this because, as everyone knows, unemployment has dropped in one month by 150,000, and that is the greatest drop ever known in a single month. Therefore the reasons for opposition criticisms of the budget are fast disappearing and when unemployment no longer presents a formidable problem I just wonder what the opposition will have to talk about.
In conclusion I would like to renew my congratulations to the Minister of Finance. He understands the economic problems of our country and has taken steps to resolve them. I am sure the methods he has used, some of which are already in effect and have brought results, will solve our economic difficulties, and they do present a logical answer to those difficulties. For these reasons I submit that the subamendment 57071-3-1051
The Budget-Mr. Meunier and the amendment should be defeated, and that the resolution of the minister should be supported by this house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is customary for the Minister of Finance, when making his budget speech, to deal with all matters relating to the welfare and progress of our country.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) called the budget a sick budget. Personally I think it is a lame budget because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) forgot to deal with an important matter concerning all provinces and more particularly the central provinces. I refer to federal provincial tax arrangements which have been talked about for a long time and to which no final solution has yet been found. Yet, it is a matter of record that when the Minister of Finance sat in the opposition he kept promising that he would find a solution to the problem. In his budget speech, the minister merely referred to it in the following words, as found on page 1234 of Hansard: Additional financial assistance being given to the provinces will enable them to proceed with needed capital improvements in the provincial and municipal fields.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this vital question should have received more attention on the part of the Minister of Finance; he should have spoken at greater length on this subject. This matter was raised in the house about two weeks ago and it was not dealt with in a satisfactory way that would have told us what to expect, because the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) have not yet told us that they will soon call a federal provincial conference nor if they have something better to propose or to substitute for the agreements now in force, that is to say the equalization and stabilization payments.
As far as we, in the province of Quebec are concerned, a province in which this matter has been under public consideration for nearly 15 years, it would be important that we know if the government will maintain the present agreements or if it will return to the province of Quebec its field of direct taxation as requested by the premier of that province.
We have not had the pleasure of hearing ministers representing Quebec constituencies speak on this matter in this house but, in the last election campaign, we heard them say that the province of Quebec had been despoiled and done out of its rights, and that a Conservative government would restore what had been taken away from the province.

The Budget-Mr. Meunier
However, on June 3 we heard the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) make a fine legal statement to the house but, unfortunately, since he had used up all his time, we could not find out whether he approved or not of the equalization payments now in force or if he proposed something better and more progressive. I hope that before long the hon. member for Bellechasse, an eminent jurist and lawyer, will speak on behalf of the province of Quebec on this matter and inform us of his conclusions so that we may know what to expect and what is the stand of members from Quebec on this matter. I feel sure that the hon. member will speak for the province of Quebec and will say what he thinks of the tax agreements now in force, and whether he is for or against their maintenance, whether he feels that the province of Quebec should be handed back its powers of direct taxation.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of detailing the history of the tax agreements arrived at between the central government and the provinces, nor to repeat that the provinces were forced to accept these agreements, and even to sign them under duress, as has been held by some.
May I simply say that the provinces were by no means obliged to accept the proposed agreements, whose object and aim was to apportion between the provinces the income accruing from direct taxation provided by income tax, corporation taxes and succession duties. It seems that if certain provinces were not satisfied, all they had to do was to levy taxes inside their own borders on the three bases which I have just mentioned and to reject the suggested agreements.
These agreements were arrived at in order to prevent double taxation and to bring relief to the Canadian taxpayer.
It is recognized, under our constitution, that the federal government and the provinces have a concurrent right to direct taxation and the hon. premier of Quebec has at last acknowledged that principle, which he was the only one to reject, since, in 1954, in enacting his own provincial income tax law he had inserted in the bill a preamble stating that provinces had priority over the federal government in the field of direct taxation. Later on, however, he withdrew from that stand by deleting those words about priority.
This principle being acknowledged, Mr. Speaker, what was the aim of the federal government in seeking to reach an agreement with the provinces about direct taxation, and how did the federal government happen to get involved in that problem?
This very complex question is a result of the 1930 depression when the prairie provinces, unable to face their obligations and

bending under the load of unemployment relief decided to ask for the assistance of the federal government.
At that time, all provinces were anxious to stop unemployment but, unable and unwilling to do anything, they stated one after the other that unemployment was a national problem, which came under the federal government. This was the time when groups of unemployed marched on Ottawa to force the government to action.
In times of depression and trouble, Mr. Speaker, all problems are referred to the central administration, but in times of prosperity and abundance everyone claims more than his own share. Following that economic depression, the Liberal government, which was back in power in 1935, instituted unemployment insurance and, as everyone knows, millions of dollars are spent each year for the administration of that social security legislation. The provinces did not help the central government at all in the administration of that legislation; however, the federal government must have the revenues required to make it work.
After the 1930's, the Liberal government instituted old age pensions and the provinces gave their approval. Later on, the central government advocated the establishment of arts and trades schools and subscribed a large part of their cost of construction without any protest on the part of the provinces. Later came subsidies for the construction of hospitals, subsidies for public health, pensions for the disabled and the blind and also family allowances. There, again, there was no protest from the provinces, as far as I know, against such steps. For these reasons, I have said and I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that if the obligations of the federal government have no limits, its powers must also be limitless.
Everything is being laid at the door of the central government but, on the other hand, everyone wants a large share of its revenues without wondering whether the central government will be able to meet its undertakings. Let me recall some facts which give a good illustration of this.
A few years ago, when cattle suffering from tuberculosis had to be slaughtered as a measure of protection for human beings, and to keep our livestock healthy, by which government was the job done, and who paid a compensation to our farmers for their losses? It was the central government, and no province protested.
When, a few years ago, an epidemic of foot and mouth disease broke out in the west, in Saskatchewan, what government sent men to destroy the affected cattle, and who paid

an indemnity to the owners? It was the federal government who was involved, with no help whatever from the provinces.
If, for instance, an epidemic broke out tomorrow among cattle in this country, and cattle had to be destroyed and an indemnity paid, who would be called upon to pay the shot? Again the federal government, and the provinces would claim that it is a matter of national concern and not their responsibility.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I have demonstrated to a certain extent what are the central government's obligations to the people of Canada, which this government has to fulfil lest it be charged with neglecting its duty. However, to fulfil these obligations the federal government must count on certain revenue.
I claim moreover that the Liberal governments which administered this country for 22 years have always worked with the very best intentions and made serious and sincere efforts to solve any difficult problem. I would hope that the present government will continue along the same lines.
In 1955, the Liberal government proposed equalization and stabilization payments which constitute an equitable distribution of wealth and revenues throughout this country in order to help the poorer, less fortunate provinces. This is a problem which occurs in any federal system, and the government must act in a way that will safeguard national unity and allow every citizen to share equally in the common wealth.
It has been only in the last few years that the two richest and most highly industrialized provinces began to show a desire to break their ties with the central government, without renouncing their rights or privileges. They wanted to avail themselves of their abundant revenues, taking no account of the rest of the country.
Have they forgotten that if they are prosperous and if their industries are thriving, it is because they sell their products in the other provinces? For instance, how many billion dollars worth of agricultural equipment have they sold to the prairie provinces, when we know that certain highly mechanized farms use $20,000 to $25,000 worth of agricultural machinery? How many billion dollars worth of furniture, electrical appliances, cars, radio and television sets, etc., etc., have the central provinces sold to the prairie provinces? It is the sale of these goods manufactured in the central provinces, that keeps their manpower at work and brings them very substantial revenue.
The Budget-Mr. Meunier
Equalization payments were instituted by the Liberal government in order to correct the situation and allow the citizens of less favoured provinces to attain a level of prosperity and wealth equal to that of other provinces.
We do not know the final policy of the government on this matter. However, the Prime Minister stated in Winnipeg during the last election campaign that his party, while in opposition, had criticized not the principle of sharing the federal treasury with the provinces, but the extent of that sharing, as regards payment of funds to provincial governments. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), taking the floor on this question on June 2 last, emphasized the needs of the provinces rather than equalization payments.
However, the promise was made during the last election campaign that a conference would be held between the federal government and the provinces to settle this problem once and for all.
When will this conference be held? We do not know yet but, as representatives of the people, we should like to know.
We know the attitude of the premier of Ontario, Mr. Frost. He stated that he was not satisfied with the agreements developed in 1955 and proposed smother formula which would bring his province 100 million dollars annually, an amount, he said, the province needs. He took part in the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958 and stated that he would get what he wanted.
I said at the outset that this question has been discussed in the province of Quebec for the past 15 years and that the premier of Quebec, the great champion of the rights of his province, always stated, outside the conferences in which he took part, that he would obtain for his province what had been taken away from it. Of course, he was never clear and precise on this matter and never made concrete suggestions that would lead to a solution of this problem. I just said that the premier of Quebec stated outside of the conferences that he would obtain for his province what had been taken away from it. However, when he comes to Ottawa, he does not speak that way and merely repeats what he said in some previous conference.
Indeed, if we refer to the proceedings of the 1957 conference, we see that the premier of Quebec repeated the same vague and indefinite proposals he had submitted at the 1955 conference. The conclusions of the brief submitted by the province of Quebec are summarized as follows:

The Budget-Mr. Meunier
(a)	qualification and delimitation of the powers of taxation of both the federal and provincial authorities, in accordance with the letter and spirit of the Canadian constitution, that is to say having regard to the past, the present and the future;
(b)	simplification of public taxation in such a way as to reduce its cost and facilitate its collection;
(c)	moderation in the domain of taxation to be arrived at by the collaboration of all public powers, in such a way as to ease the burden of the taxpayer so far as possible.
As we can see, Mr. Speaker, the position of the premier of Quebec was always vague, confused, indefinite. And I might add that his motivation was very simple: those proposals were made by a Liberal government and the premier of our province wanted to play petty politics instead of working for the progress of our country.
Now that the Conservatives are in power and that the sworn enemies of the prime minister of Quebec are in the opposition, he might modify his attitude and show himself in a more conciliatory mood; in fact, for the last year we have not heard those sarcastic statements on autonomy, on the protection and retrocession of our rights.
Moreover, since the Conservative members from Quebec who were elected to this house have fully agreed with Mr. Duplessis on the question of tax arrangements, would they be so kind as to tell us if they approve equalization and stabilization payments that were introduced by the Liberals but maintained by their own party until now, and approved in principle by their chief, the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) ?
Could they suggest any better and more concrete way of restoring to Quebec all it was deprived and despoiled of, as the leader of that province used to say?
They did however promise, through the ministers representing constituencies of the province of Quebec, namely the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois), that everything the Liberal government had taken away by way of taxes and rights would be returned to the province of Quebec.
If there was a gross injustice, I ask that the situation be settled at once and I urge the Minister of Finance to call a federal-provincial conference immediately to that end.
Besides the Conservative members from the province of Quebec who advocated that doctrine during the election campaign-I talked about it a moment ago-during that

same period, the Minister of Finance himself stated in the province of Quebec that the provinces could expect justice in the field of taxation. The Minister of Finance came to my riding, in Montreal, on the 18th or 25th of March 1958, and said that the problem would be solved to everyone's satisfaction. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that at the time a wave of conservatism was sweeping over my constituency. After the visit of that hon. minister, where he stated that everyone could expect justice and that the difficult question of taxation as well as that of tax agreements would be settled, I began to gain ground and I was re-elected with the rather comfortable majority of 4,000 votes. I therefore thank the Minister of Finance for his help and I am grateful to him for it. The hon. minister had insisted on that question but he does not seem very anxious now to call a conference with the provinces. In fact, his delay in fulfilling a promise made during the last election, his silence on this subject in his budget speech and the humility for which he is well known lead us to believe that he is satisfied with the way in which the tax problem has been settled in 1955 and that he feels unable to bungle that lasting Liberal piece of work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising to take part in this debate I should like at the very outset to add my congratulations to those which have already been extended to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for having brought down this realistic budget, his first budget, and the first Conservative budget for over 20 years. I should like to congratulate him on the courageous attitude he has taken and the measures adopted to combat and overcome the many problems which face our economy at the present time. I should not wish to miss the opportunity of saying that for the most part these are problems which were inherited from the previous administration as a result of certain policies set out by that administration during its last days in office. I refer specifically, of course, to the tight money policy. Let me quote from the budget address of the former minister of finance as reported on page 2216 of Hansard, March 14, 1957. Mr. Harris said on that occasion, and I quote:
The same excess of demand for goods and services was also reflected in a "tight'* credit situation. The monetary policy of the Bank of Canada has been one of restraint, and the fiscal policy of the government has worked in the same direction.

This was the policy of the former Liberal government the members of which party are today speaking diametrically opposite to that policy. So that there may be no confusion in this matter, let me point out that Mr. Harris in his speech that day went on to say:
It is true that the Bank of Canada could have further increased the supply of money and credit.
But, Mr. Speaker, they did not do this although the former minister and his colleagues were well aware of the repercussions of their actions as exemplified by a still further statement on the part of Mr. Harris as reported at page 2216 of Hansard of that day when he said:
Higher rates of interest have given encouragement to saving, have moderated a certain amount of spending and have caused some capital programs to be postponed.
Let us consider the effect of this policy on municipal governments in Canada as an example of the problems which resulted from such a policy in all spheres of the Canadian economy. In discussing this problem I will use as an example the municipality of metropolitan Toronto with whose problems I am more closely acquainted. This municipal government is operating at the present time on a ten-year plan of capital expansion to cost about $1 billion or approximately $100 million a year. It is proposed to finance about $90 million worth of capital works every year. Despite the high credit rating which this municipal government enjoys both in Canada and in the United States there has been an increase of 2 per cent in the cost of its capital financing and it becomes obvious that a 2 per cent increase in the interest rate on $90 million of projects over a period of 20 years will cost the people of this city $18 million over and above what this financing would have cost if the tight money policy of the previous Liberal administration had not been in effect. Besides this $90 million of capital works program which is debentured over 20 years, as a rule, the people of the metropolitan area of Toronto are taxed in addition with a special two mill capital levy which is collected out of current taxation and which amounts to over $6 million a year and is in effect a device being used by this particular municipal government to overcome to some degree the effects of the tight money policy.
It is not to be wondered that the government of metropolitan Toronto has requested special aid from this government to assist in the building of the proposed east-west subway in the city of Toronto, a project which
The Budget-Mr. Kucherepa is estimated to cost about $200 million. The effect of the tight money policy on this project alone, over and above the ordinary debenture charges, will be to add $40 million of cost to this undertaking calculated at the rate of 2 per cent per annum as I have outlined. As a result of this kind of difficulty many public works have been postponed as was predicted by Mr. Harris in March of 1957, and as a result of this postponement the number of unemployed has increased.
The latest results of this tight money policy, I submit, are manifested by the greatly reduced numbers of supporters of that former government sitting in this house today. At this time I should like to make a suggestion to the government with regard to the financing problems facing all our municipalities. There is a statute known as the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 183 which provides for loans to municipalities by the federal government to enable a municipality to pay the whole or any part of the cost of constructing or making extensions or improvements to or renewals of a municipal waterworks system, a municipal gas plant, a municipal electric light system, or other municipal project, if the project to be constructed or the extensions or improvements or renewals to be made will be a self-liquidating project, and if the project is urgently needed and will assist in the relief of unemployment for the municipality. Any application by a municipality under this act requires approval by the lieutenant-governor in council for the province and requires a municipality to obtain an undertaking from the province that the province will guarantee to the government of Canada the payment of interest and principal of the loan.
Under this act the interest on such a loan is at the rate of 2 per cent per annum, payable semi-annually, and the loan is to be amortized by semi-annual payments sufficient to pay off the loan during a period fixed by the federal government and such period is not to be longer than the estimated life of the project. This act to my knowledge has never been implemented. I should like to suggest that the government investigate the possibilities of this act having in mind that it was passed in 1938 and therefore might be in need of revision in so far as the aggregate principal amount of loans made under its authority is concerned as well as other items which may be desirable to change at this time.
I should like to take this opportunity of commending the government for the speedy action it took in again amending the housing act, early in this session. I believe this will

The Budget-Mr. Kucherepa help not only to solve some of our housing problems but will also help to relieve some of the unemployment, the roots of which this government inherited from the previous Liberal administration, whose unrealistic tight money policy did so much to create this unfortunate situation.
In September 1957 the new Conservative government made $150 million available for loans on mortgages to stimulate construction of houses, under the National Housing Act, in the fall and winter months. Subsequently, another $150 million was made available, making a total of $300 million in 1957. When the Conservatives took office in June 1957 the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had no funds left for new commitments. The new national housing bill which the Conservative government introduced, while not changing the old one in principle went a good deal further to meet the needs of certain people, needs which had not been met in the past.
The effect of this new legislation has been, as was intended, to induce others to lend money under the act and to stimulate construction of low cost housing across Canada. The former Liberal government up to the time of the 1957 election, had not proposed any such amendment; on the contrary, their "tight money" policy ruled out any such possibility. Today they are critical of what the Conservatives did, and did at once on taking office and are continuing to do, as evidenced by the amendment brought in early in this session in this very important field of housing.
Much has been said by members of the Liberal party, regarding the lack of a budget during the last session. I wonder if my hon. friends in the Liberal party are aware that the last Liberal budget was for the fiscal year 1957-58 which did not end until March 31 last. So when hon. members of that party reiterate the question of why there was no budget brought down in the last session, they are in effect arguing that the last Liberal budget should have been scrapped or amended because of its shortcomings.
For the purpose of the record I should like to point out that the Liberals themselves did not feel obligated to present a budget when they called parliament into session on March 19, 1945, and dissolved it on April 16, 1945, with no sign of a new budget to succeed the last previous one of June 26, 1944. Nor was there one until October 12, 1945. The Liberal government in 1944-45 went 16 months without a budget whereas the present government has been in office less than 12 months and has brought in a budget and this in

addition to a financial accounting given by the Minister of Finance during the last short session of parliament.
Much has been said by opposition members regarding the lack of tax cuts in the budget before us. They seem to have lost sight of the fact that in this budget the following tax cuts are included which were not present in the 1957-58 budget. The excise tax on automobiles has been cut by 25 per cent, from 10 per cent to 7i per cent, at an estimated cost of the treasury of $20 million for the full fiscal year 1958-59. In the field of personal income tax, reduction exemptions for -children were raised $100. One effect of this will be to free completely from income tax some
100,000	taxpayers. It will also give relief to about one and three-quarter million others. In a full year, the cost to the treasury will be about $60 million.
There has also been a reduction in the tax on income in the first two brackets of the income tax structure, which will benefit every taxpayer in Canada, particularly those whose taxable income is not more than $2,000 and that constitutes about 70 per cent of the taxpayers in this country.
A change was made in the corporation tax rate structure which will be of particular benefit to small corporations, although all corporations will receive a measure of relief. The lower rate of taxation, 20 per cent of profits, which used to apply only to profits of $20,000 or less, has been extended to apply to profits of between $20,000 and $25,000. Some 2,000 corporations which fall into this category will have a tax on profits within this range reduced from 47 per cent to 20 per cent. The cost to the treasury in the full fiscal year will be about $21 million.
The government's plan of spending many more millions on pubic works is obviously a very sound approach to the problem of unemployment. While the government has already cut taxes from the former high Liberal level, the government's public works program does not anticipate the effect that higher spending may have on industrial production but goes to the core of the problem at once. Besides, tax cuts bring immediate relief only to those paying taxes and it is the unemployed, not the taxpayer, whose need is most urgent today.
The Conservative government's tax reductions, higher pensions and abolition of artificial credit restrictions have been helpful, but their full effect has not yet been felt. In the same way, the full effect of the Liberal government's economic mistakes took some time to become evident, and even now in some degree these effects are still with us.

The acceleration of useful public works is, indeed, one of the recognized methods of inoculating and boosting the economy with the resultant increase in employment, trade and prosperity. People of the Toronto area are happy indeed that a substantial works program will be carried out soon in this locality. This program will provide essential public buildings, airport extensions and harbour improvements. More than $15 million will be spent in the metropolitan area and this should help not only to keep employment at a high peak but also to provide for the necessary improvements required to keep pace with the rapid development of this vital area of Canada.
The improvements to Malton and Toronto island airport at a cost of $4,335,000 are long overdue and have been a matter of great concern to the council and people of this area. The expenditure of $4,440,000 will bring about those necessary improvements and repairs to the Toronto harbour, which will provide the important facilities, so essential to accommodate the increased industry and commerce which will result from the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway.
The $5.3 billion budget which is being proposed-the largest in the history of this country in peacetime-will go a long way in stimulating our economy and helping to overcome the problem of unemployment. This sum does not include such items as the government's liabilities under its guarantee of insured loans under the National Housing Act and the variety of other disbursements which altogether are also working toward further stimulation of the economy of this country by this form of public investment. In the past year this amounted to $447 million, which moneys are available from the repayment of loans, insurance and pension accounts receipts and other non-budgetary sources, as shown in the white paper. This year this requirement will reach $755 million. This infusion into the economy should also be a stimulating factor in promoting a higher level of prosperity.
This should certainly satisfy some, if not all, of those critics in the opposition groups who have been asking what this government intends to do for the solution to the problem of unemployment, which I again reiterate was inherited from the previous Liberal administration which refused to recognize the warning signals and which took a course directly opposite-

speechtext:
I am referring to notes because of the technical nature of the subject
The Budget

Mr. Kucherepa which I am now discussing. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the previous Liberal administration refused to recognize the warning signals and as a result of this took a course directly opposite to that which they were advised to take and as a result of that we find ourselves in the present economic dilemma which faces this country.
The members of the opposition made much of the present unemployment situation in Canada and yet in March 1955 when there were more than 400,000 people out of work the same Liberal party did not consider this to be a major problem. To summarize the situation, I should like to refer to page 3556 of Hansard of January 21, 1958, and the remarks of Mr. Solon Low, who was then leader of the Social Credit party in this house and a veteran of many parliaments, who had a full opportunity to observe events in this house for many years. He said:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I have conducted ourselves all through this session as if we believed what I have just said. Now the Leader of the Opposition is asking the government to resign and give over the reins of government to the Liberal party without an election. As I think about that I remember how indifferent the Liberals were on several occasions to high unemployment during wintertime. They claimed it was seasonal and regional and temporary.
Those terms-seasonal, regional and temporary- have been so burned into my conscience that I shall never forget them. When I bear in mind the fact that it was either policies instituted by that party or things they left undone which started this country into stagnation and carried it before last June 10 quite a way down that road; when I think of the tragic decline in farm cash income during the past six years; and when I add to these things the fact that the Liberal party got as far out of touch with the people of Canada as they did, I And it difficult to see for Canadians any advantage whatsoever in a change of government at this time from Conservative to Liberal.
These were the words of the leader of the Social Credit party who sat in this house during the last parliament and indeed they well summarize the situation as to where the roots of this unemployment problem might be traced.
Some hon. members imply that one of the main causes of unemployment in Canada is the suggestion to divert some 15 per cent of our purchases from the United States to the United Kingdom. Mr. Speaker, these hon. members claim that the Americans have reacted by cutting their imports from us. Similarly, perhaps they would have us believe that United States factories have closed down, leaving millions of workers idle because of this suggestion of increasing our trade with our oldest and perhaps one of our best customers in years gone by.
All this talk about United States reprisals is nonsense. The United States buys from

The Budget-Mr. Kucherepa Canada only what they have to buy. Fifteen per cent of our sales from the United States are made up of five main items. Most of the rest that Canada sells to the United States is made up of raw materials needed to keep United States factories going. Obviously, any reduction of these imports would mean idle workers in the United States, and conversely an industrial slow-down in the United States is bound to reduce demands for those Canadian products. This government has nothing but the friendliest feelings for the United States. Our efforts to expand trade with the United Kingdom were never directed against the United States but were aimed at serving the best interests of Canada. It would be in the interest of Canada to expand our trade with the United Kingdom because this would allow Britain to buy goods from Canada with those dollars.
Mr. Speaker, I submit the Liberals had every opportunity to foresee the current trade recession with its resultant unemployment. What did they do? They did nothing. If anything, through their fiscal policy they contributed to it. The fiscal policy outlined in Mr. Harris' budget speech in 1957 confirms this statement.
Some Liberal members criticize the government for policies that they think are harmful to our relations with the United States and at the same time they suggest that Canada should use as a bargaining device our cooperation with the United States in questions of hemispheric defence. I cannot help but quote the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the remarks he made on May 13, 1958, as reported at page 25 of Hansard, and which are as follows:
We must naturally protect our interests when they are prejudiced by United States policy. We must, for instance, make it quite clear that the United States cannot expect full and complete co-operation in continental defence, which is desirable, if she treats us unfairly in her tariff and trade policies.
I submit that this kind of Liberal policy as enunciated by the leader of that party is not worthy of one who has had such vast experience in the field of international affairs and who should realize the serious implications of such a move. It is certainly not a matter for bargaining or bartering for special economic considerations which, I am sure, can be achieved through friendly negotiations between the governments of the United States and Canada.
I should like to refer now to the Liberal amendment which was in these words:
This house regrets that the government, in its budget proposals, has failed to cope satisfactorily with the problems of the recession in spite of the largest peacetime deficit in Canadian history and that it is moving towards greater trade restrictions


at a time when other countries in the western world are moving in the opposite direction.
The Liberal amendment before us is most incongruous. On the one hand, it criticizes the government for failing to take steps in fighting the recession. I presume what is meant by that is increased spending as suggested by the Liberal party during the recent election campaign. Their propaganda, as manifested by the crash program of $400 million of further tax reductions plus a six weeks tax holiday, seems to indicate to me that this is their thinking on this matter. Yet in the same breath the amendment implies criticism of the government for spending too much when it refers to the largest peacetime deficit in Canadian history. It appears to me that whoever masterminded this amendment does not believe in the maxim, "you can't have your cake and eat it too".
The second part of the amendment is also ambiguous and without too much meaning when read in conjunction with the statement of the Leader of the Opposition made on May 13 last to which I referred a few moments ago. If I may refresh the memories of hon. members, this is the way it went:
We must naturally protect our interests when they are prejudiced by United States policy. We must, for instance, make it quite clear that the United States cannot expect full and complete co-operation in continental defence, which is desirable, if she treats us unfairly in her tariff trade policies.
This statement implies that the United States is unfair to us in her tariff and trade policies. This, of course, is contrary to what the amendment contains when it says, "that it"-meaning the government-"is moving towards greater trade restrictions at a time when other countries in the western world are moving in the opposite direction." So, Mr. Speaker, the amendment does not seem to have very much in the way of substance when it is so incohesive.
The C.C.F. amendment, of course, can best be understood in the light of the sum total of the remarks made by members of that group, especially in the light of the remarks made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), who on the one hand referred to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) in the most derogatory terms and on the other hand alluded to the kindness of the Soviet ambassador in Ottawa in affording him a free plane trip to British Columbia. In the light of this kind of thinking, there is not much point in discussing their amendment.
This debate affords me an opportunity to discuss another matter of international importance. We in Canada are of necessity spending many millions of dollars on defence each year while the international situation

remains tense and strained, no worse and no better than it has been for some years.

speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the western world has developed powerful military alliances which today are the greatest deterrent to war and aggression and which will continue to be essential for some time to come in maintaining the liberty and freedom which we in the western world still have with us today.
It is true that world peace now rests on power so threatening that neither side dares to use it. That being so, what we need now more than anything else is to return to that kind of rational thinking through which, by sincere inquiry and debate, we can distinguish the true and the false, the right and the wrong.
We must not take a defensive position on these international matters but we should bolster our now strong military alliances by furthering economic co-operation with our allies and other free countries to a similar degree so as to counteract the new challenge in the field of trade. Apparently the Soviet government believes this to be our vulnerable position. Therefore we should not hesitate to take steps to ensure a strong economic front among the free countries of the world at the earliest possible opportunity.
At the same time we must demonstrate that our values and ideas, shared by millions of others, represent a positive way of life based on great traditions of truth and justice which have been recognized as the unwritten international law throughout the centuries. This should be the basis of our thinking. I cannot help but reflect upon the inspiring words that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom uttered in this house on June 13 last, and I quote from page 1151 of Hansard:
The Budget-Mr. Kucherepa
You may ask how will it all end. X do not believe that we need fear the future if we hold firm to our faith and our ideals. In time even the monolithic dictatorships crumble and change, for although the free world by its very diversity often seems weak, in its variety and above all in its freedom it is fundamentally strong. I do not believe that a purely materialistic concept of life will forever satisfy men and women; nor do I fear a continuing struggle of ideas. This I think should be our chosen battleground.
If we can measure up to this conception in international affairs, then I believe that we will be able to solve the problems that confront us in the world today. Without this kind of foundation, neither meetings at the summit nor conferences in the capitals of the world can bring us enduring peace or security.
What we need today is to respect those international institutions such as the United Nations where debate can take place and where truth must eventually come to the fore. We must not be too eager to exchange the role of the United Nations for that of summit conferences. When we did that in the thirties, when we abandoned the League of Nations and pinned our hopes on a kind of summit meeting, the results were disastrous. The proper place and the best place for our deliberations on these vital matters is the United Nations, in full view of all the nations of the world. Summit conferences should be complementary to the United Nations but should not become a substitute for the United Nations.
In a way, time is on our side. It will not be the number of guided missiles or any other armament which will determine our future. It will be our spirit and our devotion to the principles of democracy and Christianity, upon which our traditions are based and from which our progress has stemmed. True, we must maintain our defences for some time to come and we must also expand our economic alliances and meet the challenge of assisting the hungry free nations of the world.
Recent events in Hungary only underline the situation as it exists in eastern and central Europe today. There, many races, enslaved by communist tyranny, look to us in the west with hope that justice will be done and that liberty will once more assert itself in their midst. We must never become complacent, self-satisfied or apathetic if we are to maintain our liberties and also be of service to those less fortunate than ourselves who are today the victims of brutal communist subjugation.
Then, in the battle of ideologies, ours will triumph because it has stood the test of time whereas the communist philosophy, being what it is, will disintegrate, disappear and

The Budget-Mr. Forgie go the way of all dictatorships. When this happens, our various efforts within the commonwealth, in NATO, in the United Nations and in other similar undertakings will be crowned with success and will help to achieve freedom and enduring peace, not only for ourselves but for those many nations now enslaved by international communism.
