Mr. Speaker, I would like to read from the eighth paragraph in the speech from the throne as follows:
You will be asked to approve a number of measures and appropriations to continue and extend the program of my government in sustaining employment by the acceleration of useful public works and by encouraging the development and processing of our natural resources.
I have listened to most of the debates which have taken place in this house since the presentation of the budget but I have yet to find a clue as to what policy the present administration intends to follow with respect to unemployment. The administration now in power must cure the unemployment situation; the responsibility for this matter is squarely on the shoulders of this administration and it must now prove its worth.
Unemployment was not an issue in 1957 when the Liberal administration was in office. In this connection I would like to refer to the statement of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made when he was a member of the opposition party during the year 1955. This statement bears repeating, and the minister said at that time-
When we entered this debate several weeks ago l am sure that all hon. members expected that the government would avail itself of this opportunity to make an announcement of whatever policy it proposed in order to grapple with a situation which is assuming emergent proportions.
Then he went on to say:
This session opened 2i months ago with a statement by the government contained in the speech from the throne as follows: "Some employment of a regional and seasonal nature is being experienced".
As has been said, the Minister of Finance has described the present unemployment situation as a fairly mild recession. He must accept full responsibility for that statement, made at a time when there were over 500,000 people out of work. This budget brought down by the Minister of Finance is a political expedient but the administration has been unable since 1957 to find a solution to the problem of unemployment. If this were not so we would not have had a march on the parliament buildings such as we experienced yesterday. Those unemployed people returned to their homes frustrated and disconsolate.
This is a serious matter but the present administration is seemingly living from day to day and it might be said that their motto

is: seize the day and trust as little as possible to tomorrow. The public expects the administration to solve the problem and while public works will be of assistance such relief would only be temporary and the unemployed need permanent jobs. Such permanency can only be attained by a reduction in personal and corporation taxes with a consequent expansion in trade. Such tax reductions must take place now when industrial profits are dropping and our unemployment is the highest in history. The cushioning effects of extended benefits are now disappearing, thus increasing the hardships of the unemployed.
We find on the order paper a resolution to increase the capital of the Canadian farm loan board. That is apparently as far as the resolution goes and the government seems to be awaiting a debate on this resolution in order to formulate a farm policy. In the speech from the throne we read of amendments to certain acts but up to now there is not one inkling of any realistic approach to a practical farm policy.
So that the farmers of our nation will not conclude that the Liberal party has nothing constructive to say on this question I wish to present in brief form, as my time is limited, the salient features of our policy in this frightfully important matter. We shall be interested to hear from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) with respect to the farm policy of the government. At page 1892 of Hansard of March 5, 1957 he is reported to have said:
I think there is no question that one of the most serious features of our whole agricultural economy and set-up at the present time is that the great majority of farmers now are getting in the older age brackets. The number of young farmers is comparatively small, and the reason for that essential!: is the extremely high cost of buying and equipping a farm at the present time. It is impossible for a young man with a very small amount of capital to go into farming as it was possible, and as thousands and hundreds of thousands did, 50 or 60 years ago.
If our agricultural economy is to continue on a sound basis it is essential that we get more young men into agriculture, and that can only be done if funds are made available to young men, who are interested in the agricultural life to purchase and equip those farms. I know the present act is not adequate to do that to anything like the extent that is necessary.
From the findings of the Gordon report and the submission to the government by the interprovincial farm council it is apparent that our farm population is steadily declining. In 1840, 70 per cent of the population of Canada was engaged in agriculture; in 1940 the percentage was 33 per cent, and in 1956 it was 13 per cent. To most of us these are startling figures. I do not think we can ignore the fact that the notable prosperity arising from the rapid development of our country during the past 20 years has

by-passed the farms. There are different phases of agriculture in Canada-the mari-times with their emphasis on products other than grains; Ontario and Quebec with their mixed farming; the prairies with their overwhelming stake in wheat; and British Columbia of course, with its emphasis on fruits.
The export markets have not treated our farmers too kindly. What of the future? On page 159 of the Gordon report we find this statement:
We have already expressed the opinion that, in time, price and other changes in U.S. agriculture may bring supply and demand sufficiently into balance so that agricultural surpluses will cease to be chronic.
That may be overly sanguine but it would stretch even the limits of our optimism to believe that over the next 25 years the U.S. farmers will be so powerless, the inducements offered them so slight, and the remedies applied to overproduction so drastic as to leave much room in the U.S. market for increased imports of Canadian foodstuffs. At the present time, however, it would appear that our farmer will enjoy a good export market in the United States for beef cattle for the next four or five years unless hit by a tariff. Livestock and livestock products are by far the largest source of income to Canadian farmers. They yielded $854 million in 1955. The estimated cattle population in 1957 was 10,293,000, and the hog population 5,160,000.
To improve farm conditions and to enable the farmer to obtain a greater share of our prosperity, the Liberal party enunciated a farm policy in January of this year which was reiterated and enlarged upon by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) at Cudworth, Saskatchewan on February 27. The government must come to grips with and solve this serious problem that is facing the farmers of both western and eastern Canada. These problems are not identical, however, for the western and eastern sections of our country. They are not even identical in the three western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I should like to read a paragraph from the Gordon report at page 175, as follows:
Adjustment of farm organization and farm production to changing economic circumstances, including changing technology, will also, in our opinion, call in some instances for rather more generous credit arrangements than are now available. Too easy credit can aggravate farm problems by inducing an expansion in output that would lead to lower prices. Scarcity of credit, on the other hand, can prevent a desirable rise in agricultural productivity by perpetuating antiquated types of farm organization. As the mechanization of Canadian farms continues, some farmers in all parts of the country will need more medium-term capital to enable them to buy machinery and equipment, and more long-term capital to enable them to enlarge their holdings.
The Budget-Mr. Forgie while the rise in demand for meat will mean that more capital will also be needed for the purchase of livestock. As the result of these cumulative developments, the capital value of farm businesses will be rising on the average; and there will be difficulty in transferring them from one owner to another-in many cases it will be from father to son-unless somewhat more generous credit arrangements are available. So long as farm incomes are relatively low and irregular, it is important that fixed annual payments on mortgages and other forms of indebtedness be no larger than is necessary. Appropriate rates of interest will vary from time to time, but annual payments can be reduced by extending the number of years over which the principal will be repaid. Since the long-range prospects for farm income and for the ability of farmers to service loans would seem to be favourable, we think that farm credit agencies might appropriately extend the period of repayment up to 40 years for long-term loans and up to five or six years for medium-term loans. Extension of credit on somewhat easier terms is one way by which the adjustment of Canadian farming to changing economic conditions can be facilitated. Another way is by altering the emphasis of research programs. In view of the heavy demand that is anticipated for beef and other livestock products, it would seem sensible for research programs to stress the improvement of beef cattle, feeding for beef production, of forage crops, and the carrying capacity of grasslands.
As I see the requirements of western Canada they are as follows:	First, there is
increased population by immigration. In 1957, 282,000 immigrants entered Canada, a greater number than in any other year since 1913 and brought the post-war total up to 1,700,000. Had it not been for this powerful addition to our manpower, Canada would not have progressed and expanded in the way in which it has since the war. In the next quarter century Canada will need all the morally, mentally and physically healthy people who will wish to come to our shores. It will be interesting to see what will happen this year. If the British immigration figures for 1958 mean anything, we shall surely scrape the bottom this year.
The second requirement is mixed farming that will result when immigration is stepped up, particularly in western Canada. That should reduce wheat productions. The third requirement is the establishment of industries and the fourth is the development of a leguminous rotation cash crop as, for instance, soybeans, particularly in Saskatchewan.
The government must provide funds to accelerate research in order to provide, particularly in Saskatchewan, a profitable leguminous cash crop such as the one I mentioned, namely the soybean. For this crop particular types of soil are required. Such a crop would be the answer to the wheat surplus problem provided that research will develop a seed that will ripen before the arrival of the early frost that sometimes hits Saskatchewan in August. Much research has already been done in this line. I have

The Budget-Mr. Forgie been advised by the authorities that a grant of $20,000 a year would be sufficient for this purpose.
A study of the European market requirements will reveal that there is a market in Great Britain and in Europe today for over 100 million bushels of soybeans. The last shipment of soybeans exported from Ontario to Germany was sold at $2.55 a bushel. The highest yield in Ontario, as far as I know, has been 69J bushels to the acre obtained on Pelee island in lake Erie. Practically all the soybeans now grown in Canada come from western and southwestern Ontario. In 1936 about 1,000 acres of soybeans were grown in that section of the country. Last year the acreage was 264,000. An additional 4,000 acres were grown near Morden, Manitoba but the difficulty has been that the oil content has been somewhat low and the average yield has been only 12 bushels to the acre in comparison with 24 bushels to the acre in the province of Ontario last year. However, research is being carried on at the University of Manitoba and has been going on for some time in an effort to secure a better type of bean for that section of the country. Also I am advised that soybeans have been grown near Saskatoon and Indian Head.
The oil development which played such an important part in adding to Alberta's prosperity pinched out in Manitoba, so that diversification of the economy in Manitoba had to be sought by other means to give it a broader base. Agriculture still is the underpinning of Manitoba's economy, with better than 49,000 farms being worked and with production worth $248 million last year. But there is considerable diversification here, with substantial production of crops other than grain, and with livestock accounting for close to half of recent annual returns. Farm income has not increased substantially, but farming has become a dependable business rather than a hazardous occupation.
The big bonanza for Manitoba has been growth of manufacturing. In the past seven years expansion in this area of the economy has been of the order of 40 per cent, with industrial production exceeding $700 million in value last year. Some 1,650 plants give employment to more than 50,000 people of a provincial population of 850,000.
Significant as to what happened is the increase in the production of metal and mineral products, which had a value of $77 million in 1951 and last year was worth $145 million. Wood products, chemicals, electrical apparatus and building materials also have shown spectacular growth. The people of Manitoba have good reason to be

proud of the achievements of the post-war period and the consolidation of it in the last few years.

speechtext:
The dynamic factors in the agricultural picture of the future will likely be technological improvements, growth of the domestic market and conservation. Scientific farming, with proper care of the soil and careful choice of the crops, will play a leading part in increasing and maintaining output.
Farm problems of east and west are similar in the matter of financial assistance that should be given by federal and provincial governments. I do not suggest that all assistance to farmers should come from the federal government, Mr. Speaker. I think the provinces will have to co-operate as the provinces of Quebec and Ontario are doing at the present time.
To assist the farmers throughout the country, we in the opposition feel that certain steps must be taken that will not only yield a higher financial return to the farmers but will strengthen the family farm and conserve and improve the fertility of farm lands. Acting on this belief we passed, a resolution in January of this year to provide all possible help to farmers to improve their economic position by expansion and extension of existing farm credit facilities at present provided by the Canadian farm loan board, the Canadian Farm Loan Act, the Farm Improvement Loan Act and the Veterans Land Act into a complete program of short-term, intermediate and long-term credit.
Such a program would make readily available, at low interest rates, adequate long term capital for farm improvement, the maintenance of the family farm as a healthy economic unit, the purchase of farms by qualified young farmers with small cash payments, and the consolidation of farms. In the estimation of many this program would revolutionize farming in Canada. And, as I said, great emphasis should be placed on agricultural research to find methods of improving and diversifying farm products and introducing new species and new techniques and lowering costs.
To carry out this program for credit assistance we would establish a farm development bank. This bank would control and coordinate all government activities in this field and supervise the loans except those under the Veterans Land Act. That would involve removing the farm loan board from the Department of Finance and placing it and certain

other credit functions under a farm development bank directly responsible to the government.
This farm development bank, combined with improved research and proper land use, expresses our basic policy for the long term improvement of the position of all sections of the agricultural community.
We would also like to make it easier to improve farm homes. We think the time has come when more should be done for rural housing than has been possible in the past. We think that because of the rapid growth of our towns and cities there has been, perhaps inevitably, in recent years too much concentration on government assistance for urban housing. That certainly was a vitally important problem at the time and in some parts of Canada it still is, but surely there is an urgent need to improve housing in the rural areas and small towns.
In reading speeches made by members of the house in 1956 on the Canadian Farm Loan Act, as well as the discussions that took place before the banking and commerce committee, I would think it is fairly well agreed: first, that the loans should be increased to 75 per cent of the appraised value of the land and the maximum amount of the loan increased to $20,000. Second, that regional advisory boards of not more than three members should be set up by the farm development bank to hear applications and question applicants for a loan. Authority to set up one board in each province is contained in the 1935 amendment to the Canadian Farm Loan Act, but one board for each province is inadequate. Third, that the appraisal staff should be increased, and, in this connection, I think all those in the agriculture committee, and the majority of the members who spoke in 1956 and 1957, are of the opinion that V.L.A. appraisers should and could be used by the farm bank.
In the administration of the V.L.A., supervisors call on the veterans in their district from time to time and assist young farmers by way of advice and suggestions. They are well trained men with good judgment. Good public relations such as exist under the V.L.A. are most desirable in dealing with farmers. As I said, V.L.A. appraisers could be used to assist appraisers appointed by the farm bank.
Small farms form part of our sound social structure and should be encouraged, and the operators should receive adequate government assistance, both federal and provincial. The government must do all in its power to prevent a further decline in farm population. If we desire to keep our young people on the
The Budget-Mr. Forgie farms, we must give them some encouragement, especially in the form of adequate financial assistance.
The splendid state of affairs under the Veterans Land Act is in large measure attributable to the field men or supervisors of the V.L.A. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) in his address at Edmonton in May said:
Undoubtedly a good deal of the credit for this fine record belongs to the V.L.A. field supervisors, who have become experts in advising the settlers on how to use their resources to the best advantage in order to neutralize, to some extent, at least, any unfavourable prices for farm products.
V.L.A. officials are presently engaged in a survey to determine what is needed to improve the incomes of our full time farmers. So far they have analysed reports on the farm business of over 3,000 settlers and have found that the key to the problem for most of them is more capital. The survey is continuing, and we are studying the possibility of making more supervised capital available to these farmers.
Full time farmers under the V.L.A. are being well served. Loans under the Veterans Land Act are showing a decline, and before long these appraisers and supervisors could be absorbed by the farm development bank that we have previously advocated. Last year 2,400 full time farming loans under the V.L.A. were paid off and there were only 435 new applications. So, Mr. Speaker, the work of the V.L.A. appraisers is on the decline.
The lapse of time is too great from the date of the application to the completion of processing the loan. That delay is caused mainly through the scarcity of qualified appraisers. As for the processing of the loan, there are delays beyond the control of the board. These delays have all been set out in the banking and commerce and the agriculture committees. There is no need to repeat them. Long term loans and low rate of interest on capital invested in farming is the hard core of the problem of financing agriculture, particularly young farmers starting to farm.
The amount of capital a farmer needs to reach reasonable efficiency varies from $10,000 or $15,000 and in many cases more. Agriculture represents immense long term capital investment. Recent estimates put the value of Canadian farms and buildings, implements and machinery and livestock at $10,000 million. Land is normally a nondepreciating asset, except, of course, when the farmer neglects his soil by failure to fertilize or properly rotate his crops. Livestock represents a semi-permanent investment since it may be renewed by reproduction. Farm machinery is subject to depreciation and obsolescence and, consequently, loans should be for a short term only. Lower rates

The Budget-Mr. Forgie of interest and longer periods of repayment are essential to start a young man on the farm.
It has been pointed out by the chairman of the Canadian farm loan board that 25 per cent of the loans have been made for the consolidation of debts and it may be that there has been a significant increase in loans for this purpose. If so, this is a condition that must be seriously considered. Many of these farmers really cannot make a go of it because their acreage is too meagre or the amount of livestock inadequate to operate economically.
Today, banks and mortgage and insurance companies can find more lucrative and less risky loans than farm loans, and hence a farm development bank would soon become the only practical source of credit for our farmers, and especially of long term credit with low interest rates. And I may say, judging from the comments of farmers for whom I have acted in connection with Canadian farm loan board loans, that they are satisfied with a ceiling of $15,000 to $20,000. In an effort to have loans processed in the early spring farmers should be urged to have their applications in a month or so before the snow comes, and all appraisals should be completed before that time. This is not insurmountable.
In my riding many farmers work out after harvesting at carpentering and other jobs. Their take-home pay is substantial but, as the chairman of the Canadian farm loan board said, there is no objection to that so long as the operations of his farm do not suffer. In fact, in the Canadian Farm Loan Act a "farmer" is described as one whose principal occupation is farming.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, while all those recommendations are worth while, we in the opposition stand firm in our conviction that until there is a consolidation of the different legislative enactments aimed at improving the lot of the Canadian farmer through the establishment of a farm development bank and supervised loans no effective and satisfactory economical results can be attained for the farmers of our country. The small size farm is so necessary in Canada. Few of us would like to see small farms replaced by corporate farming. When a farm development act is established and operating we shall witness a lasting improvement in farm conditions and farm economy and a general upsurge in business throughout the nation which will result in restoring employment to a vast number of unemployed, and thus fulfil a two-fold purpose.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other members who preceded me in this budget debate, and even before that, I wish to express to the chairman of the house, to the deputy chairman and to yourself, their assistant, my congratulations. I could not omit congratulating the two new ministers.
As mayor of a municipality, together with those in this house who fill the same post in the province of Quebec, may I say to the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) how much the union of county councils of the province of Quebec, of which he is the president, feels honoured for the confidence shown him in his appointment as Minister of Defence Production.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that it is to me a great honour, one shared by my family, to be sitting in this House of Commons as member for the constituency of Portneuf. I therefore sincerely thank the electors of that constituency for this mark of confidence and assure them of my whole-hearted devotion to their interests for the duration of my mandate. The last time that this constituency was represented by a Conservative member was in 1882, but there is no doubt that, in future, with the progressive and reassuring policies of the present government, under the talented and wise leadership of its valiant leader, the Conservative party is assured of the confidence of the people there for many elections to come.
My congratulations go out also to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for bringing down a budget in keeping with present economic conditions. The budget provides large expenditures for public works designed to increase employment and to remedy that deplorable condition of unemployment due to the lack of foresight and to the inertia of the former administration.

Because of my experience in the municipal field, I feel it was a generous move to exempt municipal corporations from the sales tax on materials used in the setting up of a fire-fighting system and other systems under municipal control.
Mr. Speaker, as was noted by several newspapers, it has been very rare that any part of a budget speech has been given in French, as was done by the Minister of Finance. That, to me, is a source of great satisfaction.
I would now like to give a few facts concerning the constituency I represent. Geographically it is only a few miles southwest of the old historic city of Quebec, which is now celebrating the 350th anniversary of its founding. The constituency is bound on one side by the north shore of the majestic St. Lawrence, over a distance of about 40 miles, between Grondines and St. Augustin. On the opposite side is the Laurentian mountain range covered with a great and rich variety of timber which contributes to the operations of several sawmills and pulp and paper mills of the area.
The population of this constituency is evenly divided between farmers and industrial workers. From the agricultural point of view, large scale farming is the main activity. Dairy products are processed there for marketing purposes, either into butter or into powdered milk.
I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to express to the government all my satisfaction and that of the agricultural organizations which forwarded me some resolutions about the Agricultural Stabilization Act enacted by the last parliament. Particularly in so far as my constituency is concerned, I am very proud to extend my congratulations to the government, about the very satisfactory level where the guaranteed price of butter has been set for the next year.
I wish to point out that some communities of my riding specialize in the production of potatoes, that the maple syrup industry means a rather important supplement to the revenue of many farmers and that the setting of a support price for each of these two products would be desirable and would contribute to a more stable revenue to which the farmer is entitled since he must set his budget for the whole year, not to mention that it would remove his uncertainty about future markets. I also express the wish that a serious study will be made with a view to setting a support price for pulpwood derived from family wood-lots, a product which is also an essential factor in the revenue of many of our farmers.
The Budget-Mr. Rompre
A few years ago, the federal government was helping the maple syrup producer by paying him a subsidy representing one third of the purchase price of aluminum pails. That subsidy is still paid in the same amount by the provincial government and there again, Mr. Speaker, I express the wish,-it is also the wish of many maple syrup producers,- that this subsidy will again be granted. The restoration of that policy would substantially help that class of farmers and would at the same time contribute to the production of a better quality product, that would fetch better prices.
There are in my constituency a few communities where farms are not favoured with a loamy and very productive soil. Although I am no expert in this field, I nevertheless wish to refer to some suggestions made to me by several owners of such farms, to the effect that a grant for the claying of their land would be of great help since it would contribute to increase productivity and help them derive a better income from this land.
There is in Portneuf a provincial forestry school where, each year, sons of farmers follow seasonal classes. I feel that it would be wise to encourage by grants the reforestation of some parts of the unproductive farms, as this would create a substantial asset for the coming generation.
With regard to industry, I must point out that the working people in my constituency are mostly employed in pulp and paper mills as well as in a number of sawmills. The lumber industry which feeds these other operations constitutes a rather important source of employment.
There is also, at St. Basile, a cement plant that turns out a good quality product. That industry is only a few years old and is very prosperous.
The quarries of Riviere-a-Pierre provide a granite of incomparable quality, and similar products at St. Marc des Carrieres are another source of employment for our workers. As was done by my good friend, the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Letourneau), I draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) on that fact and I express the hope that these localities specializing in the production of cut stone will be called upon to provide at least part of the raw material needed for the construction of the public buildings mentioned in the estimates for this year.
I draw the attention of the government to the importation of American cut stone from

The Budget-Mr. Rompre the Indiana Lime Stone quarries. It would be desirable that steps be taken to avoid such competition which is harmful to an industry which is of vital importance to the communities I have just mentioned.
The other main industrial centres are Donnacona, noted for its paper and wall-board industry, a very fine product widely used in the interior finishing of houses and public buildings, and St. Raymond whose industry is largely dependent on forest products, as are the industries of Pont Rouge and Portneuf where similar plants are found.
The largest streams flowing through the constituency are the Jacques Cartier, St. Anne and Batiscan rivers, much used by the industries and the municipalities I just mentioned either for floating pulpwood or feeding power plants.
I am convinced that the $450 million put at the disposal of the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation at the beginning of this session by this government will greatly contribute to a revival of activity in those industries whose products are used in housing.
As regards the other communities along the St. Lawrence river, some of them are agricultural but others, for instance Des-chambault and Grondines, have been characterized for many generations as the birthplaces of marine officers such as pilots, captains and others.
May I now mention another great natural resource of the area. I refer to the innumerable rivers and lakes teeming with plenty of fish and situated in a vast forest district where game is plentiful. That makes the area very attractive to tourists.
My constituency comprises an area whose subsoil is rich in minerals and for years has been giving to one category of local labour the advantage of honestly earning its living.
I unfortunately have to regret the suspension of operations of the two mining companies which produced zinc and lead at Montauban-les-Mines. I refer to the Anacon Lead Mines Limited and the United Mon-tauban which closed down in 1955, laying off 300 of their employees.
This mining centre has become a ghost town, which gives a striking idea of the previous Liberal government's improvident and stand-pat policy which I mentioned at the ouset of my remarks. That is also an example of the heritage left to this government.
[Mr. Rompre.l
To remedy this urgent situation, I would suggest public works. I think it would be important to build a retaining wall along the north shore of the St. Lawrence river to prevent the erosion caused by the tides and by the waves in the wake of the big ships going up or down the channel. This erosion causes considerable damage to property along the shore where houses of great value have been built. This work is absolutely necessary in several parishes of my constituency situated along the St. Lawrence river. May I point out to the house that the extension of the wall already existing along the St. Anne river to protect shore properties from the considerable damage caused by floods such as the one of December last would be a great help to the people of St. Raymond.
In the field of social security, while not unmindful of the generosity of the present government during the last session, I will, Mr. Speaker, put before the house several resolutions that were forwarded to me by various executive councils of parochial associations in my constituency requesting the government to pay family allowances up to 18 years of age in respect of children who continue their studies. Needless to say, I share those views. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that steps such as this would be of financial assistance to parents and would advance the cause of education. Another important social security measure would be the payment of a pension to widows and single women at age sixty. These people have a great deal of difficulty in finding employment, and special attention should be paid to their needs.
These remarks that I have just submitted to the house, in the course of which I have advanced a few suggestions with regard to the solution of problems which are of particular interest to my constituents, were offered in the hope of making a modest contribution to the work of this house, in order to attain that object which we all pursue in common, that is to say in order to ensure the greatest possible degree of wealth, prosperity and security for all our fellow citizens. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that with the sincere and conscientious co-operation of all members of this house we will, in fact, reach that goal.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sometimes wonder who has the most difficult task in a parliament, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Leader of the

Opposition (Mr. Pearson) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). Quite bluntly, I think I have to come to the conclusion that the man who has the most difficult task in a parliament is the Minister of Finance. He is damned if he does, and he is damned if he does not. As far as the present budget is concerned, he is going to have to be damned because he does not.
I think all of us have either read or listened with a great deal of interest to the statements of cabinet ministers at various times. We listened to and read the speech from the throne, and I have listened to, read and reread the budget speech. My own feeling on the matter is that I find it difficult to understand just what is government policy. I am inclined to the belief that cabinet ministers are trying to ride two horses at the same time. I have oft-times seen this done by acrobats at circuses but I do not think it has any place in politics or in parliament.
Over the weeks, if not over the months, the Prime Minister has been trying to impress upon the Canadian people the need to spend, to spend and to spend, and I can understand- we can all understand-his thinking in that regard. Undoubtedly he is motivated by the thought that if the people of Canada will just spend and spend the money will go for capital purchases in part but consumer goods in the main and heavy expenditure by the people on capital purchases and consumer goods will so lower inventories that the factories can commence to roll at full speed again and consequently our basic resource industries also. As I said, that can be understood with that motivation if we do not tie it in with the budget of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance, in contradistinction to the economic policy of the Prime Minister, has announced a deficit on current expenditure in the next twelve months of some $641 million. In addition, he quite honestly tells the house that in the next twelve months the government will have to go to the people for loans amounting to close to $3J billion. I think I am correct in saying that in a speech recently the Minister of Finance said that in all probability borrowing approaches will be made perhaps once a month.

speechtext:
That is a nice way of getting out of it, but because you cannot meet your maturing bonds you have got to borrow in order to cover them. It still amounts to the fact that the government is going to the people of Canada for this amount of money which has to come from two sources. You cannot lend money to the government and at the same time spend it on consumer goods. The two are diametrically opposed. As far as I am concerned, I admit that I am completely confused by what appears to be a confusing and contradictory government policy.
I also find myself hoping that the optimism of the Minister of Finance is well founded but I wonder whether he can back up his optimism with the opinions of Canadian economists and the pronouncements of government departments. I think the Minister of Finance must have an entirely different crystal ball from that of the majority of economists in Canada. The minister was kind enough to inform us that the $641 million anticipated deficit in the current budget was forecast on the basis of a two per cent increase in the value of the gross national product. We sincerely hope he is correct but I think we are not being unkind by drawing to his attention that if he is wrong Canada may find itself in a most difficult financial situation.
The daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics for Monday, June 23, contains information relative to the gross national product for the first quarter of this year and indicates that there has been a decline of almost two per cent. Although we have not seen any indication of the required policies yet, I know the minister will realize we are very sincere when we say we hope that during this session the government will be

The Budget-Mr. Winch able to announce policies which in the remaining three quarters of the year will be able to overcome the two per cent deficit in the gross national product in the first quarter and achieve the two per cent increase the minister referred to in introducing the budget the other day.
There is something else a number of us would like to have clarified, the position of the government with regard to trade. I know that I am not the only one in the house or in Canada who is still very confused as to what is the government's trade policy. If we listen to government spokesmen outside the house I am certain we all get the impression that the government believes in freer trade and also gives some indication of tending toward free trade. But inside the house the budget appears to indicate the maintenance of the proverbial Conservative protectionist policies. I am not going to speak at length on this matter at the present time. I sincerely hope that when the necessary resolutions and bills are before the house we will be able to have a clear exposition of the principles underlying the trade policies of the present government.
At this point, and because it comes to mind, may I discuss something which disturbs me greatly as I am certain it does the Minister of Finance also. I tried to get some indication of the minister's feelings the other day through questioning but I am afraid that perhaps it was not the right place for me to raise the matter. I refer to the fact of the government introducing tax reductions and some people then taking advantage of them and not passing them on to the ultimate consumer to whom I am certain the minister wants them to go. I am sure that is definitely what the minister has in mind when he introduces tax reductions. I also think that the majority of people in Canada carry them out but unfortunately a great many do not. Of necessity I had to make a hurried trip to my home city of Vancouver last week end. While there I met friends of mine in the retail trade and what did I find? The minister brought down his budget on a Tuesday. In his budget he removed the sales tax on cut flowers.
The next day right in the city of Vancouver, the growers-not all of them it is true but some of them-increased their prices by the amount of the sales tax they had taken off. I do not imagine there is any kind of law which this parliament could pass which would take care of a situation like that but I would certainly like to have a very, very strong statement from the minister as to what in his opinion might be done to stop people from doing this kind of thing. If they persist in what is tantamount to absolute

dishonesty, then perhaps we could work out a method by which we could publicize their names so that the consumers would no longer buy their products and maybe that could bring them to task.
I feel certain that a great many people in this country were disappointed in the budget as recently introduced, disappointed because neither the budget changes nor the allocation of the estimates conformed, by a long shot, with what the people of our country had been given to understand they could expect from the Conservative party when its first budget was introduced in this House of Commons.
Firstly there is nothing in the budget in the way of estimates which gives any indication of increases in allowances for the veterans of Canada. I have not forgotten that changes have been made in the past two or three years but I also remember the statements of certain Conservative members that the increases were not half enough and that the veterans were entitled to a better deal.

Do you call that a new deal for the veterans? That is very interesting- the legislation we had last session was the new Conservative deal for the veterans. In that case many thousands of veterans in this country must have been very disappointed for I am certain they all had a very different impression of what they might expect. They got a raw deal instead of a new deal. The fact that there is nothing in the estimates over and above the legislation to which I have just referred is, in my opinion, not only a dereliction of duty and responsibility but is a major disappointment to the Canadian veterans.
These remarks apply also to the plight of the senior citizens of Canada. There is nothing to indicate any further assistance to this group and presumably the legislation introduced last session was the new deal of the Conservative party for the old age pensioners. There is nothing in the estimates to indicate any improvement. Given all the commendation that is due for the increases and changes made during last session we still say that this parliament is unfair to the senior citizens of our country in allowing them to continue living on a semi-starvation basis. There is nothing so far as I can see which is proposed to bring the purchasing power of the dollar in line with the pensions of this group of people. There is a responsibility on the shoulders of the government, with its huge majority, to see that our senior citizens are cared for. Even though the government will not go as far as spending more money

to help the older people surely it could bring in additional legislation, over and above that introduced last session, to allow old age pensioners to draw their pensions outside of Canada beyond a period of six months.
I find it difficult to understand why we have laws in this country, and a government which permits such laws, under which a former official of this house who cannot return to Canada without facing a criminal charge can draw his pension in the United States for the rest of his life and yet an old age pensioner cannot do likewise. Surely if one has served his country so that he is entitled to a pension he should be able to spend his days anywhere in the world with his loved ones, and still receive his Canadian pension. Other pensioners can do so, so why cannot an old age pensioner? Such a measure would cost this government only an infinitesimal amount with respect to administration costs in order to give that right to the people who need it so much. It is not, after all, asking for very much but I defy any member on the government side to give one logical reason why it should not be done and we hope it will be done at this session.
I do not like going back over the years but we must remember the position of our civil servants in respect to superannuation and how it was said by Conservative members that the previous government was unfair to them, that something ought to be done for them and that something would be done for them. We were told how they would get a new deal from the Conservatives but as yet we have no indication, as a result of legislation or in the estimates, that anything is going to be done this year to bring our retired civil servants-our servants-to the position where they would benefit from some form of equalization in respect of their pensions and the purchasing power of their dollars-something else which was left out.
