speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing my remarks on the budget I should like to join with hon. members who have spoken previously who expressed their disappointment that there is nothing in the budget to indicate that the government has any intention of increasing the family allowance.
I believe it is a great disappointment to all people that the government has not recognized that there is a responsibility on its shoulders to so raise this allowance as to combat the loss in the purchasing power of the dollar. I do not intend to repeat arguments that have already been voiced but I do want to draw the attention of the government to a discrimination which we feel strongly should be removed as speedily as possible. I refer to the fact that for some strange reason the law with regard to the family allowance was so drawn that the families of our personnel in the armed forces do not receive the allowance if their families join them overseas. I raised this matter before in committee and was informed that this action was not the responsibility of the Department of National Defence that the situation exists because of a specific section to that effect in the Family Allowances Act. We have been told by officials of the Department of National Defence, however, that perhaps one reason people in this position are denied the family allowance is because of the additional help the families receive when they are sent overseas to join the head of the family. We maintain that this point of view cannot be substantiated in fact.
I am not referring to the 700-odd members of the armed forces who are now overseas attached to embassies, attaches or NATO headquarters because they are well taken care of through financial assistance which in the case of a person who holds the rank of lieutenant-colonel is as much as $190 a month. I am referring to the 11,000-odd armed service personnel overseas who do not fall into the categories I have mentioned. I have been informed by the Department of National Defence that a great many of this number are married and their families are overseas.
I was surprised to learn on what basis they receive an additional allowance. I was advised by the department this afternoon that the increased allowance for families of our armed service personnel overseas is based on the figure established by the dominion bureau of statistics relating to the cost of living wherever the family is stationed as related to the cost of living in the city of Ottawa.


It works out this way, just to put it rather briefly. If the personnel is stationed in the United Kingdom and living in what is known as married quarters the bonus is nil. If they live outside married quarters the amount is $10 a month for each family. If they are stationed in Germany and are in married quarters the bonus is $15 a month and if they are outside married quarters it is $30. If they are stationed in married quarters in France and have the rank of lieutenant-colonel they receive $48 a month. In the case of a private the amount is $32. A lieutenant-colonel living outside married quarters receives $100 and a private receives $64. I want to emphasize the fact that according to the information given to me only this afternoon these amounts are all based on the dominion bureau of statistics calculation of the variation in the cost of living in the various centres I have outlined as compared with the cost of living here in Ottawa. On that basis, therefore, we can see no reason for the discrimination against the families of our armed service personnel overseas who are no longer entitled to draw the family allowance when they leave the shores of Canada.
Armed service personnel overseas are required to pay income tax under the provisions of that act which is only fair and just but they should likewise be entitled to receive the family allowance. I sincerely hope the government will recognize the injustice of the situation as it exists at this time and will take action at this session to remedy the condition I have drawn to its attention.
There are many other matters which I know are a disappointment to the people of this country in that they have not been included in the policy pronouncements of the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. It is to be sincerely regretted that apparently no action is to be taken to establish a plan and policy under which financial assistance could be given to the municipalities at low interest rates. The government is to be commended, of course, for the action it has taken in the removal of sales tax from certain equipment when purchased by municipalities and which will result in a saving to them this year of approximately $5 million but the municipalities are in a desperate situation and require a great deal of money with which to carry on the services they provide. It would have been of great assistance had the government indicated that action was being contemplated at this session in this regard.
As I have already indicated there are a number of matters which I have not yet discussed but I feel it is sufficient for one to

speak for 25 or 30 minutes and the other matters I have in mind can be discussed when the estimates are before us and so I will conclude with this statement. In all probability this house will be sitting for another two or three months and so there is still plenty of time for the Minister of Finance to redeem himself in the eyes of the public. I think all the people of Canada-and I know all hon. members of the opposition-are so broad in their outlook and generous in their hearts that they will overlook the minister's sins of omission if he will now come forward with the estimates and proposals that will not only meet the expectations of the Canadian people but will also represent the fulfilment of Conservative promises.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like my first words in this house to be words of congratulation to you on your election to the high office you hold, and may I extend the same compliment and my good wishes to the Deputy Speaker and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea). I wish also to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on his budget. It was a delight to me not only to have been present at its delivery but to have felt that in some small measure I was a part of it. I say a part of it because the budget sets out judiciously and exactly those things which I, as a Conservative member, support.
In the budget speech there were two statements which struck me forcibly, the statement on distress selling and that on fair value for duty. In these two clear, concise statements of broad principle may be found the hope for a solution of a long-standing problem in my constituency, that is the plight of our fruit and vegetable growers.
Before dealing specifically with these two budget statements I would like to sum up a few points which apply to my riding. To me, Okanagan Boundary is a lovely part of the world with fertile valleys, forests, lakes and rivers, all set in the heart of the mountains in the interior of British Columbia. I like to call it home. As other members speaking of their constituencies like to call their own places home, so also do I.
As for industries, we have mining, lumbering, ranching and fruit and vegetable growing. We also have a well-established tourist industry. In one respect at least, the province of British Columbia has taken a back seat to no place on this continent and that is in providing campsites and picnic grounds. These are readily available along the highways and beauty spots of the province. They are well laid out camps, with all the facilities provided. Here I would like
The Budget-Mr. Pugh to commend the federal government for the financial assistance they have given to the provinces aiding construction of such camps.
In Okanagan Boundary there is one further aid to our tourist business which I hope the government will take into consideration. We have a great need for the building of small boat harbourage and launching sites. Not only will this be of benefit to people locally but in general to the many visitors throughout British Columbia, the rest of Canada and from the United States. Visitors bring all types of craft and boats to our lakes. To understand this need it is necessary to know that Okanagan lake provides no safe anchorage in the form of natural bays. In each case the construction of a breakwater is necessary as a protection against strong winds. The building of breakwaters is a federal responsibility but it might well be worked out with provincial or local authorities. Here I would like to say a word of thanks for the recent action of the government in extending and modifying the present breakwater at Penticton.
While commenting on tourism, I would like to draw the attention of the government to the development of highway No. 97 which starts in California and runs up through my riding of Okanagan Boundary and the ridings of Okanagan-Revelstoke, Kamloops and Cariboo and farther on up north. Of great importance to the future is the fact that this highway, if developed further, will provide a logical link to the north. It is the shortest route with the best gradients available and apart from the tourist business, has tremendous trade and military value.
Let me say a few words on flood control. The government has, in conjunction with the province of British Columbia, done extensive work to control flood conditions on the Okanagan river. The worth of this project is shown by the additional acreage made available. Previously the river had snaked its way through the valley and now many miles have been cut off its course. Flooding of a large acreage has been cut to a minimum. However, there is need of a further study in the Similkameen valley and on both forks of the Kettle river. In the mountains fertile land is at a premium and each year erosion is taking place at an alarming rate, particularly so in those parts which I have mentioned.
I would like to turn to some of our industries. Historically, mining has played an early and important part in our growth and economy. Present-day prices for metals have forced once profitable operations to close and I regret the decision to close the mines at Copper Mountain, Hedley and Greenwood.

The Budget-Mr. Pugh This stoppage has been felt keenly through- These industries, along with fruit and vegeout my riding. We live in hopes that more realistic local legislation and higher world prices will lead to further exploration in the area.
There is one point that I might mention at this time and that is the number of young men who have completed their university courses and are prepared to go into the mining field, but mining is being curtailed in my riding and also throughout the rest of Canada, which means that there are no positions available for them. I would suggest to the government that long-needed surveys be carried out to provide work for those people to keep them here in Canada. We have had far too many moving out of our country to get jobs elsewhere.
I should like to say a few words on lumbering. Lumbering flourished in the early days. Perhaps the word "flourish" is an unfortunate one but at the same time I think it is sufficient to say that our mills have grown, that the forests are being utilized and that many men are being employed. Because of weather conditions- and I might say here that we have an ideal climate in Okanagan Boundary-our mills were able to operate with little interruption throughout the year. However, the bulk of our product must be sold to the United States and a poor market there price-wise means stocks of lumber lying unsold in our yards.
And now a word about cattlemen and poultrymen. Our cattlemen and poultrymen are producing under considerable hardship. We have plenty of room for furthering both these industries in the Okanagan Boundary area. However, our main trouble is the laid-down cost of feed grain. It is more than a little hard to know that our competitors can obtain feed grains for one-half the cost that it is available to us. For instance, we pay approximately $60 a ton; our competitors elsewhere in Canada obtain the same feed grains for $20 a ton. I would recommend that where grain is required by cattlemen and poultrymen for feeding purposes it be obtained through the wheat board at the prevailing door-to-door price in the wheat board area. It does seem to me ridiculous that our great overload of feed grain cannot find its way to a legitimate market such as this. May I here commend the prompt action the government took earlier this year to protect our poultrymen against the United States invasion of turkeys at distress prices.
I have mentioned mining, lumbering, cattlemen and poultrymen, Mr. Speaker.

tables, suffer from our position in the mountains. The common problem to all our industries, and indeed to the future location of any industry, is one of freight rates. Not only must we ship to distant markets but the necessities coming to our area suffer from a heavy rail bill, a heavy additional toll. This adds to our cost. We are in a somewhat different position from that of eastern Canada because we are a long way from a large population centre. For instance, Vancouver is 300 miles away from the Okanagan valley. We have to ship a long way. We have no market close at hand and it means the rail bill is a heavy one. The resulting costs of transportation are nothing less than a slow process of strangulation.
May I now refer to our fruit industry. My remarks will apply equally to the vegetable industry. We grow wonderful fruits and vegetables but in order to avoid any argument I will simply say this: they are second to none. Over the years our fruit industry has expanded and improved its product. Every effort is being made to keep up to date in quality and variety. We have an industrywide marketing agency. By-products have been developed and in this respect a great deal of credit is due to the experimental farm at Summerland. Perhaps a few words here will give the house an idea of the tremendous behind the scenes work which has helped our industry keep up to date.
In the beginning we planted our whole area entirely to fruit and fruit designed for the fresh fruit market; that is, fresh fruit for the consumer but we soon developed annual surpluses and we had to look elsewhere. The fruit and vegetable processing laboratories of the dominion experimental farm went to work with the full support of our industry. This forward looking has paid off. We now process roughly one-third of our entire apricot, cherry, peach, plum and Bartlett pear crops. We now have products which we hope will utilize all our surplus apricots not required by the fresh fruit market. These are worth-while outlets from a remunerative standpoint.
Apple processing has remained a large problem but we actually process approximately one-third of our crop, or 33,000 tons. Apple cider, which has been newly introduced, is another feather in the cap of the farm; that is, of the dominion experimental farm. Here extensive research work in the laboratories has resulted in a fine product. The B. C. fruit processors co-operated to the full in providing material, equipment and encouragement. Of greatest importance, of course, is the fact that the industry hopes

lower grade surplus apples will be used here leaving the better grade apples to the fresh market.
The experimental farm also has provided its worth by its work on new varieties. Another important function is their fight against plant pests and disease. Here ruthless measures have to be taken and the industry supports them through the Palmer memorial research grant. It allows large scale experimentation in the orchards and gives a form of insurance against loss through such experiments. Effective sprays are developed quickly. We back our experimental farm to the hilt. It has proved its worth and brought dollars to the industry.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I summarize the major problems facing our fruit industry. Through its chief spokesman, the industry has stated that it requires consideration on four major points and, indeed, more than consideration if it is to survive. These four major points are: First, stability of returns from year to year; second, protection specifically aimed at distress selling; third, relief in freight rates; and, fourth, farm financing and farm credit.
To enlarge on these four points and deal with them in a slightly different order, I would point out that I have already made mention of freight rates and stated the necessity of an overhaul. With regard to farm financing and farm credit, to understand this need it is necessary to understand the problem of weather in relation to orcharding. The orchardist accepts normal hazards of weather. Troubles arise through early frost, poor weather when the crop is setting, improper humidity at thinning time, rain when the cherries are being harvested. All these and many more take a tremendous toll. But this is an annual problem and in all forms of farming an accepted hazard. We accept it. There is, however, a weather condition which has in many cases caused widespread disaster. I refer to the tree-killing winters commencing in 1950. This has meant a heavy drain on our resources. It has meant replanting and in many cases new trees planted have been severely damaged in the years following 1950.
The situation requires long term rehabilitation financing. This is not available through the banks. The only other source, the Canadian farm loan board, is not available either as this type of rehabilitation loan does not meet its requirements. It is a straight question of rehabilitation and I would ask the government to give immediate consideration to this urgent problem.
On the short term basis credit has been cut as a result of the poor return in the
57071-3-106
The Budget-Mr. Pugh last five years. But the combination of winter kill and poor returns has been more than the average orchardist can stand. The position has deteriorated until now many are in serious difficulty. Financing through the banks has been curtailed in many cases. Poor annual returns are the sort of thing that make any banker, even if he is a friendly type, think twice. The result has been that a large percentage of growers now work out part time or full time. This, of course, makes it impossible to maintain the orchards properly. From the foregoing you will see that our credit position needs overhauling on both a long and short term basis.
Let me deal now, Mr. Speaker, with the remaining two major points brought up by the industry, namely stabilization and protection against distress selling. We welcome the stabilization act and we look for a measure of relief under this legislation. We appreciate its intention and feel that an honest effort based on the intention will aid in partially providing the answer to stability. But this act alone will not provide the stability that the industry needs. We require the benefits of the stabilization act certainly, but we also require an effective stoppage of United States distress selling.
Let me digress for a moment. Our fruit industry is twofold, first, apples and, second, soft fruits. There is a basic difference. Our apples are an export product and sell well in the United States market. In fact, we have a premium product and we consistently get a better price than the same type of United States fruit does in its own market. That goes for both quality and grade. There is no question of our ever having tried to undersell the American producer in his own market. We do not now ask fair value for duty in this instance. It is sufficient to state that we suffer tariff-wise. But here we can rely wholly upon the stabilization act to balance costs of production in order to provide a fair return.
With regard to soft fruits, that is, peaches, pears, apricots, prunes and cherries a different situation exists. In Canada we do not produce sufficient for our own needs and that is an important point. We do not export and we annually fill our extra requirements from the United States. The problem is one of the price at which United States fruit enters our market and also the timing. United States soft fruits reach maturity well ahead of ours. Their market is saturated before we commence to pick. When the United States market is saturated their prices begin to drop in their own country and they are faced with a disposal problem. Highly perishable fruit still in great quantities must be sold. This fruit is dumped in the United

The Budget-Mr. Pugh States market. I would ask hon. members to note that they dump their own fruit in their own market and they do so at distress prices, at prices designed to clean up the crop, at salvage prices or, if you will, fire sale prices and, of the utmost importance to us, at prices that bear no relation to the United States cost of production.
The importance of these prices is seen because it is at this stage that our own production comes on our own market. Here you see the chronic disability under which we suffer. The United States fire sale price is the price at which we must begin to sell, a price at which no self-respecting United States producer would produce, let alone sell. Much more important, this distress selling becomes the controlling factor in our price structure. These imports do occur but, believe me, fruit does not have to come across our border to dominate our price structure. The threat of import is sufficient. A quotation f.o.b. any point in the United States will do the trick.
As the Customs Act now stands we are powerless. With distress imports, that is, actual imports coming into our country before relief can be obtained, the damage is done. But over and above this there is no power in the act which can stop the harmful, in fact, disastrous results of a United States f.o.b. quotation. That is our picture. It is from this set of circumstances that we seek relief. Hon. members will now see why we have taken heart at the expression of policy with regard to distress selling and fair value for duty. Here is what the Minister of Finance said while referring to unfair trade practices and I quote from Hansard of June 17, page 1246:
During the past year many representatives of Canadian industry, large and small, and agriculture, have discussed their problems with members of the government. We have been impresed by the serious difficulties that have been created for many of them by the dumping of foreign goods in the Canadian market. Such dumping may arise from a variety of causes and may take many forms. The present dumping duties section of the customs tariff together with the valuation provisions of the customs act are adequate to deal with some forms of dumping. However, they do not deal with cases where goods are being imported into Canada at less than their cost of production and are also sold in the country of export below cost.
That is precisely what I was saying before. Later the minister went on to say:
-have examined this problem with the utmost care and am satisfied that this unfair trading practice is in fact occurring, with a harmful impact on Canadian producers.
He went on to say:
Most countries which carry on substantial foreign trade have laws to protect their domestic producers against dumping. Indeed the right to take effective measures against dumping has long been a standard provision of international trade treaties including

the GATT. The government intends to defend Canadian producers against the practice of dumping, whatever form it may take. This will require the strengthening of the present valuation provisions of the Customs Act and their effective enforcement. To this end my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, will shortly submit a bill to parliament amending the valuation provisions of the Customs Act to add a provision to section 35 along the lines of the legislation in effect prior to 1948, requiring that, where appropriate, the value for duty of imported goods shall not be less than the cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit.
Furthermore may I suggest that in the proposed amendments to section 35 of the Customs Act, the representations of the Canadian horticultural council be given the full hearing and respect to which they are entitled. We should remember that this council is the Canada-wide voice of the fruit and vegetable growers and their representations should be treated in the light of the words I have quoted which were spoken by the Minister of Finance. Let them also be treated in the light of the words of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) when he stated that in his view Canada made a grave mistake in 1948 in amending the then provisions afforded by the key valuation section of the Customs Act. He might well have said that at that date we sold the safeguards of our producers.
There is nothing new in fair value for duty. We had it once and we lost it, or gave it away. The Canadian horticultural council fought for this principle in the twenties. They received it in 1930 and from 1930 until 1935 the fruit and vegetable industry had a measure of protection unequalled before or since that time. I say since! Look what has happened. In 1935 the gradual whittling away of protection began both on specific duties and on minimum fair value for duty. Year by year concessions were given and lost until finally in 1948 the Customs Act was emasculated and we sold out to GATT.
Regarding fruit and vegetables, there are difficulties in the proposed amendment to section 35 of the Customs Act. The amendments will be based on cost of production. The Canadian horticultural council, realizing the difficulty of fixing costs of production on fruits and vegetables, has suggested an additional amending clause as follows:
Sec. 35(13) Notwithstanding anything in the Act, whenever duty ad valorem or specific is imposed on any fresh or processed fruit or vegetable of a class or kind produced in Canada, where the market price in the country of export has, as the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period, declined to levels that do not reflect, in the opinion of the minister, their normal price, the minimum value for duty shall be the amount determined and declared by the minister to be the average price for the same or similar products entered at customs during the immediately preceding ten calendar years.

(14) The operation of the value for duty fixed pursuant to the last preceding subsection may be suspended by the minister in the case of such fruit or vegetable imported into any specified region or part of Canada.
There is merit in this suggested clause because in the clause the price at which imports of fruits and vegetables enter Canada is a known amount and is easily ascertained. It is a matter of record in the dominion bureau of statistics. Such a clause would settle our difficulties to a great extent. Stability should follow as result of crop disposal at higher average prices; the government would not be called upon to subsidize the soft fruit portion of the industry under the stabilization act; United States dumping or distress selling would be curbed. It might well be that growers would become taxpayers. These advantages make sense. To my mind there is a further common-sense factor. As it now stands, when payments are made under the stabilization act the government will be subsidizing United States fruit imports. Would it not be better to provide the opportunity for the grower to stand on his own two feet?
Once again, I agree with the forthright statements of the hon. member for Carleton. May I state without reservation that the fruit industry of British Columbia is an industry of long-standing growth and is properly situated. We can face reasonable and proper competition from imported goods; we are not asking to be pampered and petted by excessively protective measures. What we want is the benefit of the amendment to the Customs Act so that foreign dumping is eliminated. And I reiterate and expand the sentiments of the hon. member for Carleton -surely there is no member of this house who wants Canadian agriculture to be compelled to compete with foreign agricultural goods sold at less than their cost of production and normal profit.
I further concur with him-I too, so long as I have a vote in this house, will not vote to compel Canadian growers and agricultural workers to compete with dumped foreign fruits and vegetables.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) deserves congratulations upon creating a precedent when he spoke several sentences of his budget speech in the French language on the evening of June 17 last. He deserves congratulations not only because of this venture but because of the quality of his French. This is a praiseworthy precedent which the Liberal minister of finance in the next parliament will, I am sure, be happy to follow. Incidentally I had an opportunity to admire 57071-3-1064
The Budget-Mr. A. Brassard the minister's French last March when he did me the honour of coming to speak to the voters of Lapointe on my behalf.
I feel it is regrettable that the minister did not deliver his budget address on the memorable evening of June 10, 1957 as it was rumoured he would do. The blue suit, the blue lectern and the artificial blue carnation would have stood out the more against a red banner indicating the $100 million deficit and by such a gesture he would have given to this anniversary the real significance of the arrival of a Conservative government in this country.
While the minister created a precedent by speaking French the other evening he certainly did not break new ground in offering to the Canadian people an enormous deficit. In this he carefully followed the well-trodden path of the Conservative party, because Canada has not seen a balanced Tory budget in the last 45 years. How could the Progressive Conservatives offer us anything else because there is a contradiction in their very title. The 20,500 words of the budget speech deserves to be considered almost a work of genius. I remember, as do many others, my college years when our professors judged our essays according to two principles-their contents and their style. If I were to apply these standards to the minister's work of art I would give him, being a Liberal, about 60 out of 100 points for style and one or two for content. However, it is for another reason that I believe the minister's effort is almost a work of genius. I believe it was Carlyle, who said that genius is composed of 99 per cent perspiration and one per cent inspiration. What a pity that little one per cent of inspiration is missing in this instance. However, the minister deserves full credit for the 99 per cent perspiration which he so elegantly exhibited to us.
(Translation):
When one reads the budget speech in the official record of this house, where it is divested of the sheen and sensationalism with which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) managed to clothe it in by his intonations, his emphasis, his gestures and his rhetorical flourishes, one is struck by the absence of concrete steps designed to solve the most urgent problem which afflicts at this time so many families in my constituency and throughout this country: unemployment.
There is no word there of any reduction in tax, only ominous silence with regard to family allowances, and complete silence too with regard to federal provincial fiscal relations. There is however another thing which
1S76

The Budget-Mr. A. Brassard will strike anybody who will take the trouble to read this speech attentively. It is the government's rather guilty spirit of self-congratulation in the presence of the difficult situation which Canadians have been facing over the last few months. This feeling cannot be necessarily inferred from the words spoken by the minister, but it can be drawn as a logical conclusion from the absence of an energetic and aggressive policy designed to fight the present recession. When account is taken of the commitments made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to the Canadian people during the 1957 campaign, when he was still leader of the opposition, and if the first Conservative budget is compared with those promises, there is no escaping the fact that the government has repudiated its solemn commitments to the Canadian people. The Prime Minister refuses to admit at this time that he had in fact promised to reduce taxation by $500 million. But what did he mean, speaking in Victoria on May 21, 1957? In a Canadian press report published in the Ottawa Journal of May 22, the following sentence is attributed to the Prime Minister:
(Text):
A Conservative government would cut unnecessary taxation to promote production which would help meet the threat of inflation. Last year the government had overtaxed Canadians by $500 million.
(Translation) :
On the other hand the Victoria Times of May 22, 1957, reported as follows:
(Text):
The Conservative leader claimed that the federal government had taken $500 million more than it needed from the people of Canada.
(Translation):
What is the meaning of those words pronounced in the heat of an election campaign if not a clear $500 million tax cut. To all intents and purposes, they surely intend to give the impression that a Conservative government will not collect those $500 million which the former administration had overcollected. If that is not-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why not? Even if I am not a professor of French at Laval, I understand French just the same. If that is not the impression sought to be created by such a turn of speech we might as well forget the meaning of words right now and perhaps lay off some French professors.
What were we offered after those promises were made to the Canadian people? A $178 million tax cut by way of resolutions in the last parliament and a ridiculous $26 million

tax cut in the last budget speech. All told, it is a little more than $204 million, when the public was led to expect $500 million. As the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) so aptly put it the other day, the government or the Conservative party gave us an example of dual policy, namely a progressive policy before the elections and another one, the conservative policy, the genuine one, after the elections.
After witnessing so many examples of this kind given by politicians lusting for power, who have one policy before the elections and another afterwards, the public will end up by saying: What is the good of being interested in politics. Politicians are all of the same ilk. If we want voters to lose confidence eventually in public men,-and in saying we, I do not include your humble servant,-all we have to do is to continue acting this way for that is the best means to that end.
There is no doubt that the government should have reduced personal income tax. It was imperative, the more so since the purchasing power of the dollar has been substantially reduced, and it would have been absolutely necessary to put more money in circulation to stimulate our weakening economy. The budget offered an opportunity to increase the basic exemption, which would have been a form of a tax reduction. I make this claim first because it is absolutely reasonable,-it may perhaps not be understood by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) but it is nevertheless a reasonable thing,- and also because it was one of the main demands of the Canadian and Catholic Labour Union during the last electoral campaign and, finally, because I wish the Minister of Finance to keep his word. In March last, the C.C.L.U. asked that the basic exemption be raised from $1,000 to $1,500 for single persons and from $2,000 to $3,000 for married people. I make this request to the government with the conviction that the Minister of Finance is a man who fulfills his promises. He must surely remember what he said here, in this house, on March 27, 1956, following Mr. Harris' budget. The hon. member for Eglinton, now Minister of Finance, as shown on page 2,648 of volume III of Hansard for that year said:
The next matter to be mentioned, sir, is the income tax. It is true that the rate is unchanged. It should have been reduced. Of course, we are going to have to wait until election year for those increases in the exemptions which are long overdue.
.. .In 1953, in the general election, the Progressive Conservative party advocated in the plainest terms an increase in the income tax exemptions to $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married persons.

What then is the hon. Minister of Finance waiting for to implement what he himself advocated? If this suggestion was good, and if he believed it was good in 1953, surely it is just as good today, in 1958.
This year the government boasts of providing supplementary benefits for the unemployed, and we hear much about its public works program. As far as the supplementary benefits are concerned, there is no doubt that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) had no wish to mislead the public, but he was so vague and so lacking in clarity,-I hope not deliberately so,-that he left with the people the impression that everyone qualifying for seasonal benefits would be entitled to the supplementary benefits. The government seemed to feel that it was highly generous towards a great number of Canadians who were in dire straits.
When I went home for a few days, I met quite a number of unemployed who, after the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) on the matter, and all the publicity that was made about it, asked me why they were not entitled to supplementary benefits.
At a time when hardship has seldom been so prevalent, why did the government not take any steps to protect those who were suffering and are still suffering from the difficult situation we experience today? This is no time for arguing, and pointing an accusing finger at those we believed responsible for the situation. It is time to tackle the problem and try to solve it.
I was disappointed the other day by the answer the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) gave to an inquiry by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Descha-telets), when he said:
(Text):
What about unemployment? I will tell you plenty about it and I will make it clear who is responsible tor the present situation in unemployment before I am done if that is the issue the hon. gentleman wants to raise.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, when we come across someone who is sick, wounded or destitute, we hasten to help him out, before quarrelling with those who might be responsible for his plight.
Much has been and still is being said about public works. I now come to Lake St. John and Roberval. What has been done there? At this point I could leave the floor to my hon. friend from Roberval if he wishes to answer. What has been done in the four constituencies of my district to improve the
The Budget-Mr. A. Brassard situation? I am certainly not to be told that the contract for the runway at Alma has been or is about to be granted; I was in the Department of Transport-I was employed there for three years-when the former minister, the Hon. George Marler, announced to the previous Liberal member for Lake St. John and to the mayor of the city that the Department of Transport had agreed to build the airport in Alma. I have followed this matter too closely, on the request of Mr. Andre Gauthier, the former member, not to be perfectly aware of what has gone on, and I am now awaiting a reply from my hon. friends in the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not answer.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All that has been done up to now back home is merely what had been planned and decided by the former Liberal government.
I hear my hon. friend saying: "That is not true." I had thought that since his election he had learned how things are done in Ottawa, and among other things, that no lies may be told here. He would seem to have a very vivid recollection of the last campaign.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) felt keenly about the unfortunate circumstances of the municipalities of this country and gave the impression that he was about to solve their problems. But what concrete steps has he taken in this connection, apart from all the words which he has used to say that he was going to do something. He simply chose to announce that he was proposing to go over the heads of the provinces, that have jurisdiction in this matter, to gather together the representatives of the municipalities. And this is the man who spoke so movingly and touchingly of respect for provincial autonomy. It is still time to help the municipalities and to bring about a material reduction in unemployment, if only the government will prove its sincerity.

The Budget-Mr. A. Brassard
For instance at Jonquiere, where I live, the corporation intends to build a badly needed municipal filtration plant. More and more new subdivisions are going up all the time, and this involves very large municipal expenditures for water supply, power and sewer systems. There are also some urgent and necessary works to be carried out in the town of Kenogami. To give but one example, it will cost close to $800,000 to rebuild and improve the water system.
The town of Arvida is in the same situation. It has to eliminate at least two level crossings which have already cost human lives and it is important that those crossings disappear as soon as possible. It still has an urgent need of a town hall to accommodate its various services. It also has other important projects which, if they were carried out, would relieve to that extent the painful unemployment situation. The same urgent needs can be noted in all municipalities. I shall look forward to hearing what the hon. member for Roberval has to say in this regard.
If the government, which promised so much, gave assistance to municipalities by way of low interest loans, unemployment would be reduced substantially in all municipalities of this country and it is a truism-I use simple words now, so that the hon. member for Roberval will understand me,-it is a truism that if unemployment is reduced locally, it will automatically be reduced nationally. As this is not hard to understand I am sure the hon. member for Roberval has already understood.
There would be much to be said about this old question of the public works promised by the Prime Minister and the Conservative candidates during the last election and I regret I will not have enough time to read a very appropriate article by a most distinguished journalist, Mr. John Bird. In that article published in the edition of February 28 last of the Toronto Star, the author describes the seriousness of the Prime Minister's gigantic program of public works and does so with as much accuracy as humour. Of course, the hon. member for Roberval would have to listen to me closely when I read it because there is considerable wit in that article. I cannot however resist the temptation to read two or three paragraphs from it for the information of the house.
(Text):
John Bird, in this article from Ottawa, writes:
The Conservatives' $1,185,000,000 "works project" to relieve unemployment is just a diddle of old

figures. It whittles down to only about $50 million of new money to provide jobs. Even Tory ministers are chary of the bogus big figures now. It centres upon that $1,185,000,000 "works project" announced with such flourish and advertised as "great" and "new" from Tory platforms across the country. And on high authority, too. Here is Prime Minister Diefenbaker's own statement, broadcast over station CKY, Winnipeg, on Feb. 12: "Now what about the future? And I know what unemployment is. Ladies and gentlemen, to provide for the future of Canada and to ensure jobs, we have launched a nationwide works project for constructive works, for dividend-paying works of $1,185,000,000 of which $270,000,000 will be spent in the first three months of this year." The text is from the Prime Minister's own office. And, in due course, out from the Prime Minister's office in Ottawa came a press release giving some particulars of the $1,185,000,000 but couched in much more cautious, canny terms than those employed by the Prime Minister himself at Winnipeg or by Conservative orators elsewhere. And there is good reason for this caution in language, because that touted $1,185,000,000 is little more than the regular departmental construction estimates for 1958-59, plus $140,000,000 of CNR maintenance and construction, which last, incidentally, is a much lower figure than the comparable one for last year. In accounting for $1,185,000,000, the Prime Minister's office tabulates $106,000,000 for that fine Tory project, the St. Lawrence seaway, launched by the Liberals, of course . . . And in blowing up to inflate the figures, $40,000,000 is included for that fine Conservative works project, the Northern Ontario pipe line against which every Tory member of parliament in the house at the time quite naturally voted "no".
The article continues:
By and large, the $1,185,000,000 figure consists of the totals for construction work of various kinds that would have appeared in the regular 1958-59 federal estimates, if ever they had been presented to parliament. But by the device of failing to present estimates and failing to give the nation an accounting in a budget before the election, the Conservatives felt able to announce regular, even routine departmental expenditures, plus expenditures on such projects as the seaway and pipe line, as if they were somehow new.
And the article concluded with these words:
For assorted politicians on the hustings to play fast and loose with statistics is nothing new in the politics of Canada or any other country. What is new in recent history is for a Prime Minister of Canada to encourage such political legerdemain.
(Translation):
To put it bluntly, Mr. Speaker, the government has noisily blared away what it intended to do to alleviate the unemployment problem. It has done absolutely nothing, except stretching winter into June, if I may use the very picturesque and pertinent phrase coined by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). Yet, unemployment is still cruelly prevailing and it is not the government's public works that have produced a lowering of the statistics: it is simply the normal resumption of business. Only a month ago, there were 12,745 unemployed in our district-I mean the four constituencies-I do not expect the hon. member for Roberval to

be aware of the latest statistics, as I am not asking so much of him,- while during the same period last year, there were only 5,622.
The municipality of St. Ambroise sent me a resolution calling for help from the federal government in order to reduce the heavy unemployment. If the government helped the municipalities, St. Ambroise might immediately start building a town hall, water mains and sewers, and tackle much other work for new services. But under the leadership of a man who will surely go down in history in this field, the government prefers to just talk.
I wanted to deal at length with family allowances and, more particularly, with the extreme indifference of the government in this matter. I listened with a great deal of satisfaction and attention to the very eloquent plea of my friend, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Bacine), on the subject of family allowances and, frankly, there is not much I can add, except that the government has failed to do its duty in a serious matter. I shall refer to the requests of the C.C.L.U. and I quote the petition its officers submitted to me during the last election: "In order to restore all the social value family allowances had when first introduced, their minimum rate should be raised to $8 and the maximum rate to $13 for each child."
This was from a text by the C.C.L.U. I also received from the city council of Arvida a resolution asking me to support the council in the request it sent to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) to have family allowances doubled and the benefits of family allowances extended to all children attending school regardless of age.
At the Conservative convention of December 13,	1956, Hon. T. L. Smith stated
that the Progressive Conservative party accepts the principle of family allowances. It is being quite generous to say that one accepts this principle much as one w(ould accept the great principles of physics and chemistry. However, in the matter of family allowances, words must be followed by deeds. Of course, that is one thing I would never ask the hon. member for Roberval.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Acting Minister of Labour (Mrs. Fairclough) to kindly study the decision just handed down by justice John D. Kearny of the exchequer court in his capacity as arbitrator in a case relating to a
The Budget-Mr. A. Brassard request made by the national union of aluminum workers of Arvida, office employees' local. This was an appeal made after the case had been heard by the arbitration board at Chicoutimi.
The members of the office employees union at the aluminum plant at Arvida have their own union which has its own collective bargaining agreements with the company.
In 1957, shortly before the Arvida strike, the office employees, having discussed the matter, decided to send a delegate or representative to the talks going on at that time between company authorities and the officials of the national union of aluminum workers of Arvida.
Once work had come to a stop after the beginning of the strike, those office employees did not leave work. Rather it was the company that notified them that there was no more work for them. In other words, they were to all practical purposes forced to leave their employment for the duration of the strike.
The appeal has been maintained and the cause referred to the arbitration board. Moreover, representations have been submitted to the hon. Minister of Labour. There is another problem connected with this question of railway employees. Many of these employees, ten, fifteen or even eighteen years ago chose to work for the Canadian National because they felt that that crown corporation offered more stability than private industry. They made a sacrifice in turning away from private industry to join the C.N. so as to work, as they said, for the government because, while the Canadian National is an independent corporation, in the mind of the public it is the government.

(Applause).
I hope that there will also be applause when I have read his statement. At the end of his speech of January 14, 1955, reported on page 218 of volume I of the House of Commons debates official report, the hon. member for Broadview said:
I would therefore urge this government to stop thinking of curing unemployment merely by making adjustments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and accelerating our public works program, necessary though those measures may be. The problem we are facing requires far sterner measures. Unemployment is the barometer of economic progress within a country, and when it increases by anywhere from 40 to 100 per cent over the corresponding figures for last year it demonstrates that we are not nearly as healthy economically as we should be.
I therefore ask my hon. friend, our genial Minister of Transport, to use all his influence with the Minister of Finance to have the very sound statement he made in this house in 1955 taken into consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make my initial contribution to the debate in this house may I 57071-3-107
The Budget-Mr. Fane presume on my own behalf to paraphrase your initial statement to the other house, and remark that should I transgress the rules in any way the fault is mine alone. For the last six weeks I have sat in my place trying to emulate that wise old owl who sat nodding in an oak tree and the more he heard the less he spoke and the less he spoke the more he heard. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have heard so many words in those six weeks that I am compelled to register a few of my own and to say that my first observation is that at this level of democracy perhaps we are prone to treat the meaning of the word "parliament" a mite literally.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I add my felicitations, belated though they are, to the accolades which you have already received on your re-election as the first commoner. At the same time I must congratulate this house on having among its members one so em-minently suited for that onerous position which would appear to demand that its incumbent be endowed with the wisdom of Solomon, the patience of Job and a disposition that commands equanimity, good humour and fairness in the face of all conditions, and all this in two languages.
I would like to point out at this time that having as a child had the honour of being acquainted with that honourable and gracious gentleman who was your father, when he and my father campaigned together in that part of the Northwest Territories which is now Alberta, I know that it is not by chance that you have the necessary attributes to fill your high position with honour.
May I add my congratulations to the Deputy Speaker and to the deputy chairman of committees of the whole on their election to the posts they fill with such efficiency. I wish also at this time to convey my felicitations to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on his success in the election just past, in being returned to office with such a decisive mandate from the people of Canada and on now having completed one full year in his high office, and on having achieved in so short a time the high ideal of a united Canada.
I must also congratulate Canada on being blessed in having a native son in the person of the right hon. Prime Minister who has been able to don the mantles of those two outstanding Canadians, Macdonald and Cartier, who, over a hundred years ago, originated the Progressive Conservative party with the object of making a united Canada, a nation composed of Canadians of many national origins, many creeds and many cultures, all welded into one people and proud to bear the name "Canadian". The
1682	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fane
result of that achievement can be seen right in this house where all the major ethnic groups in Canada are represented and are all proud of the comradeship that exists between them. This achievement is more remarkable in that other parties have worked on the principle of "divide and conquer", with very marked success in the past, having stirred up regional, national and religious animosities for purely political expediency.
1 must now make a few remarks about the constituency of Vegreville, Alberta. The constituency which I am so proud to represent takes its name from the largest town within its borders. It is truly Canada in miniature because the people who live there are descendants of those hardy pioneers who came from many lands, with many cultures and many faiths and with one idea, to make a home for their families in a country where they could be free, free to own the land on which they lived, worship according to their own belief and, in short, help to establish the freedom that we now enjoy in Canada. This they did with the result that we, the descendants of those pioneers, are welded together into a nation, Canada, and we are fiercely proud to be able to say, "I am a Canadian".
Vegreville constituency is situated in almost the centre of Alberta. In order to fix its location better in your minds, may I say that the wide spot in the road that we call the city of Edmonton, our capital city, is located about 25 miles straight west. Many Edmonton citizens were raised in my constituency, among them, for example, the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Skoreyko) and the mayor of Edmonton who has made such an outstanding name for himself. It comprises an area of about 5,000 square miles which I somehow thought was quite a size until I came to Ottawa and heard the extent of other constituencies. There are about 25,000 electors with a total population of about 50,000. It contains three complete provincial constituencies and parts of four or five others.
The main industry is mixed farming, with oil activity in the Redwater and Bruder-heim oil fields. Elk Island national park lies entirely within my constituency. Last year over 183,000 persons visited this park which is the home of some 1,500 plains buffalo as well as elk, moose and deer. In the northeastern part of Vegreville constituency is situated the Saddle Lake Indian reserve which has quite a large population of our original Canadians, many of whom are veterans of the first or second world wars and some of both. There is also a chemical plant at Duvernay.
The constituency is crossed from east to west by four railway lines but the Canadian


National line that lies north of the North Saskatchewan river and runs from Edmonton to Heinsburg via St. Paul stops abruptly at Heinsburg and requires an extension of some 38 miles to connect with the Canadian National at Frenchman's Butte, Saskatchewan.
The constituency has been represented by Liberals, one U.F.A. member and Social Credit members, the last representative having been Peter Stefura, a Social Crediter, who was here only from June 10, 1957 to March 31, 1958. Before that John Decore, a Liberal, represented the constituency for eight years but he did not stand for re-election last June. Through the united efforts of a great many people from both inside and outside the constituency, I have been given the honour and privilege of serving the finest constituency in Canada for the next four years as its first Conservative member. I am reminded that one day last spring in my home town of Mundare I went to a Liberal meeting where the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) was speaking on behalf of the Liberal candidate. I had the pleasure of meeting him that day and I remember well saying to him that I would meet him in Ottawa after March 31. At that time I did not know that I would be sitting on the same side of the house on the left of Mr. Speaker but outside the black line that surrounds the opposition.
Since I am a farmer, Mr. Speaker, and represent a constituency that is 90 per cent dependent on the farming industry, I wish to place before you the reasons for the dissatisfaction of Canadian farmers in general and western Canadian farmers in particular. However, it is my personal opinion that, while something more must be done at this time to assist Canadian farmers to get their fair share of the national income, whether by deficiency payments or other methods, such subsidization on a permanent basis is not the answer to the farming problem. I believe that continual government subsidization of any business or industry tends to destroy initiative and will in time destroy the industry and those engaged in it. There will always be more and bigger demands for additional government help if the idea of subsidizing every industry continues. I see that we are travelling along a road that will shortly divide into two roads. We have our choice. One road leads to a total welfare state, that is, one with total government control, and the other road, while embracing something of the final results to be found at the end of the first road, has at its end an economy based on agreement between all levels of business or should I say all levels of life.
To get back to the business of farming, I want to make it perfectly clear at this time

that the farmers of Canada do not wish to require handouts or subsidies or whatever you may call them, but the farmers, who are the most independent group of people in Canada, want to have it recognized that they are the backbone of the country and that it is their right to have their business placed on a level with that of other businesses. All that we ask is that we get a square deal in the economy of Canada, which means that we get our fair share of the national income. This objective is a must for our government, because, as I said before, the economy of the country is dependent on its basic industry, agriculture. We do not like to be accused of begging for special treatment in order to survive but we do want it recognized that steps must be taken to see that we get what is our due. Unlike labour, the farmers of Canada do not wish to strike and tie up the whole economy of the nation to enforce their demands because when a strike is in effect the people who suffer most are the women and children and it is not right to cause hardship to people who are innocent.
The farmers of western Canada are faced with a situation where, when we sell our grain, we have to pay the freight on it to Fort William or Vancouver. In other words, we sell our grain f.o.b Fort William or Vancouver. The freight rate from where I live to Fort William is 26 cents per hundred pounds. It is deducted on delivery. It would be more if the Crowsnest rate was not in effect. It is a fortunate thing that this rate was agreed to by the government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific railway with the idea of it being in effect forever. We are also faced with a freight rate to the prairies which is higher than the freight rate to other parts of Canada. It is a well known fact that freight from eastern Canada can be shipped to Vancouver and trans-shipped to Alberta at less cost than if the shipment was made directly to Alberta. A situation like this should be corrected.
The farmers are also faced with the excessive cost of the machinery required to operate the farms. The increase in the price of all machinery required bears no proper relationship to the value of the work it is called on to perform. Something therefore must be done to bring the price of the machinery that we must have into a fair relationship with its value to the farming industry. Positive measures must be put into effect to correct the inequities in the spread between what the producer receives for his goods and what the consumer pays for them.
I want now to commend our government for what it has already done to assist the farmers and what the government proposes to do at this session of parliament. Cash advances on farm-stored grain have been a 57071-3-1074
The Budget-Mr. Fane
very great help to the farmers of western Canada. Income tax reductions, in the next year will total over $200 million. The hospitalization plan is coming into effect in five provinces on July 1, this year. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is being changed to make it more realistic and be of benefit to more people. A national crop insurance plan is being studied and the farmers will be very happy when a comprehensive plan of crop insurance becomes effective.
At the moment, because of the inequities in the business of farming, a system of deficiency payments on farm products would be of great assistance. This would be a stopgap, until such time as the government can see its way clear to institute a two-price system on farm products.
It is very heartening to note that provision is made to expand the harbour facilities at Fort William and Port Arthur for the handling of sea-going ships and that the St. Lawrence seaway is expected to be in operation next year. This, it has been stated, will increase the return in respect of wheat to the western farmer by four cents a bushel owing to the saving in freight between Fort William and Montreal. I do hope that this is correct because the farmers in western Canada believe it to be so.
I am pleased to note that the government proposes to bring into effect a Canadian bill of rights. In my opinion, such a measure is long overdue.
I may say that the government proposals for the development of northern Canada are also long overdue, because it is well known that locked in the vastness of our great northern territory are the richest deposits of minerals and oil in the world. We must develop these for the good of Canada and Canadians and make room for increased population in Canada and provide a larger market within the nation for our Canadian products. With respect to developing this country, I would refer hon. members to the address of my good friend and neighbour, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), in which he so ably set forth the situation in his constituency and further to the north. Other hon. members from northern Canada are also to be commended for the way in which they have set forth the measures necessary in order to open up this wonderful country and make its treasures available for the good of Canada as a whole.
I am very happy to notice mention has been made of a northern branch of the trans-Canada highway to serve the north central, and northern part of the prairie provinces and British Columbia. Such a highway through the Yellowhead pass would be of inestimable benefit to Canada. I would like to

The Budget-Mr. Fane
see it come through my constituency on the direct route from Saskatoon to Edmonton, which would be over Alberta's highway No. 16, and this as soon as possible.
A great deal has been said about the railway situation in northern Alberta. The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) has at times remarked on an extension to the Canadian National Railways line which goes from Edmonton to Heinsburg, through St. Paul, Alberta-a matter of about 38 miles-and the benefits this extension would provide for the people living in the country served by this railway, and also for the industry situated at Heinsburg. The first benefit to the farmers of the Vegreville constituency, who five north of the North Saskatchewan river, would be a saving of two cents per bushel in freight on their grain. I would suggest that this government very strongly consider the necessity of urging the Canadian National Railways to complete the extension of this line from Heinsburg to Frenchman's Butte. I have never been able to understand how or why this extension was not insisted upon by former governments.
As I have mentioned before, I have within my constituency the Saddle Lake Indian reserve and I may say that I have strong opinions on the way that these people should be helped to take their places as full citizens of Canada. I know perfectly well that many of them still wish to enjoy the benefits of their more or less sheltered existence, without the added responsibility of citizenship, but if this policy of treating them as children and wards of the government continues they will never be able to take their proper place in the life of their country, and to make the contribution to Canadian life of which they are capable. I think they should be permitted to enjoy full Canadian citizenship with, for some years, no restriction on the benefits they have been receiving under the original treaty.
We have heard a very great deal of talk about the unemployment situation in Canada. This is a real problem, but I would bring to your attention the fact that there are jobs for 150,000 to 200,000 workers if they would only accept work on Canadian farms. The farmers are unable to properly carry out farming operations, because of the lack of farm help, and farmers cannot compete with industry in the matter of wages paid to farm help because farmers do not get that kind of money for what they produce. Therefore, when the returns to the farmers of Canada for their products are brought to the proper level the agricultural industry will be able

to be conducted along the lines of other industries and farmers will be able to get the necessary help to conduct their operations efficiently.
The increase in benefits to veterans and their dependents through the changes in the War Veterans' Allowance Act and the legislation covering veterans' dependents are greatly appreciated by those people to whom this country owes so large a debt of gratitude.
I was very pleased to hear the Right Hon. Harold Macmillan, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, remark in this house a few days ago that the results of the visit of the trade mission sent to the United Kingdom by the present government in late 1957 were most gratifying, and that the benefits will increase as time goes on.
I now want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on having the intestinal fortitude to bring down a deficit budget at this time. This shows that our government has a full realization of the situation in Canada and is taking drastic measures to control the situation. In time of war there is always money available for everything that is necessary. A budget based on a large deficit is the normal course to follow at that time. Why, then, is it wrong to follow the same course during peace? The statement has been made so many times that there is always money to fight a war, so why is there not money for peace? Among the many things the budget provides-and I am going to confine my remarks to a very few-are the changes in the Succession Duty Act under which a widow will now have a total exemption in respect of her husband's estate of $60,000. The injustices perpetrated under the former act have always been a very great hardship to the widows and their families. I am also pleased to see provision made for deductions in respect of medical expenses. The savings to municipalities in removing the duty on culverts and machinery will be of very great assistance. The removal of duty on parts for farm machinery will also help the farmers.
In view of what I have said, I would like to suggest that this house vote against the subamendment and, when the time comes, that it likewise vote against the amendment and that the motion proposed by the Minister of Finance be approved in its original form.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government received representations from any organization or union to amend the unemployment insurance regulations so that any claimant being laid off indefinitely from his or her plant at any time prior to the normal vacation will be enabled to draw benefit for the vacation period?
2.	If so, has the government taken any action to amend the regulations as suggested?
Answer by: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Acting
Minister of Labour):
1.	The unemployment insurance commission has received no such representations. However, the present regulations provide that a claimant for unemployment insurance benefit who has been laid off prior to a general continuous holiday may be paid benefit in respect of the holiday period. There is one exception. If the holiday starts within six weeks after the commencement of the lay-off, any holiday pay received or receivable is treated as earnings for the period of the holiday and the amount of benefit adjusted accordingly. It follows that, if a claimant is not entitled to holiday pay, benefit is paid in full for the holiday period.
2.	See answer to No. 1.
